title: 4  The Noise Outsourcing Theorem
text:
4.9 Connection to Optimal Transport
The noise outsourcing theorem has a natural connection to optimal transport theory that illuminates both why the quantile function is the right object to learn and why the CRPS is a natural loss function for training. Optimal transport, originally formulated by Gaspard Monge in 1781 in the context of moving earth, asks: what is the cheapest way to reshape one distribution of mass into another? The field experienced a renaissance in the late 20th century through the work of Brenier, Villani, and others, and has become increasingly important in machine learning, statistics, and applied mathematics. The connection to our setting is immediate: the noise outsourcing map \(G^*(\tau, x)\) reshapes the uniform distribution into the conditional distribution \(F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)\), and it does so in the cheapest possible way.
The general optimal transport problem asks: given two probability measures \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), find the map \(T : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d\) that pushes \(\mu\) forward to \(\nu\) (i.e., \(T_{\#}\mu = \nu\)) while minimizing the transport cost \(\int \|T(x) - x\|^2 \, d\mu(x)\). The Kantorovich relaxation of this problem, which allows for mass splitting, leads to the linear programming formulation that is standard in the modern treatment.
In one dimension, the answer is simple and does not require any optimization: the optimal map is the composition of the quantile functions.
We motivate this with a physical picture. Imagine a pile of sand distributed along the real line according to measure \(\mu\), and we want to reshape it into the distribution \(\nu\). Each grain of sand at position \(x\) must be moved to some new position \(T(x)\), and the cost of moving it is proportional to the squared distance \(|T(x) - x|^2\). The cheapest way to rearrange the sand is the “monotone” way: the grain at the \(\tau\)-th quantile of \(\mu\) should be sent to the \(\tau\)-th quantile of \(\nu\). Any non-monotone rearrangement would involve “crossing” — some sand moving left past other sand moving right — which always increases the total cost. The following proposition makes this intuition precise.






TipProposition 4.3: Optimal Transport in 1D



Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}\) with CDFs \(F\) and \(G\), respectively. The unique (a.e.) map \(T^*\) minimizing \(\int |T(x) - x|^2 \, dF(x)\) subject to \(T_{\#}\mu = \nu\) is \[
T^* = G^{-1} \circ F.
\]


This result is Brenier’s theorem specialized to one dimension. The optimal transport map is simply the composition of the two quantile functions: first transform \(x\) to its quantile rank \(\tau = F(x)\) under the source distribution, then map to the corresponding value \(G^{-1}(\tau)\) under the target distribution. The monotonicity of \(T^*\) follows from the monotonicity of both \(F\) and \(G^{-1}\). In higher dimensions, Brenier’s theorem still guarantees existence and uniqueness of an optimal transport map (under mild conditions), but the map is no longer a simple composition of one-dimensional quantile functions — it becomes the gradient of a convex function, and computing it requires solving a partial differential equation or a linear program. This is a major reason why the quantile-based GBC approach is so natural for univariate conditional distributions, and why the autoregressive decomposition of Section 4.3 is the right strategy for extending to multiple dimensions.
Applied to the noise outsourcing setting: the source distribution is \(\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) (with CDF \(F(\tau) = \tau\), the identity) and the target is \(F_{Y|X}(\cdot | x)\). The optimal map becomes \(T^*(\tau) = G^{-1} \circ F(\tau) = F_{Y|X}^{-1}(\tau | x) = G^*(\tau, x)\). The noise outsourcing theorem is telling us that the conditional quantile function is the optimal transport map from uniform noise to the conditional distribution. This is not a coincidence — it is a direct consequence of the fact that the quantile function is the unique monotone increasing map with the right push-forward property.
A key consequence is the following characterization of the Wasserstein distance. For two probability distributions \(F\) and \(G\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the \(p\)-Wasserstein distance is \[
W_p(F, G) = \left(\int_0^1 |F^{-1}(\tau) - G^{-1}(\tau)|^p \, d\tau\right)^{1/p}.
\tag{4.8}\] The Wasserstein distance between two distributions equals the \(L^p\) distance between their quantile functions — no optimization problem to solve, just a simple integral. In higher dimensions, computing the Wasserstein distance requires solving a linear program or regularized optimal transport problem, which can be computationally expensive. In one dimension, the quantile representation gives us the answer in closed form.
For \(p = 2\), we have the Wasserstein-2 distance: \[
W_2(F, G) = \left(\int_0^1 |F^{-1}(\tau) - G^{-1}(\tau)|^2 \, d\tau\right)^{1/2}.
\] This means that if we learn an approximate quantile function \(\hat{G}(\tau, x)\) and the true one is \(G^*(\tau, x)\), then the \(L^2\) error \(\int_0^1 |\hat{G}(\tau, x) - G^*(\tau, x)|^2 \, d\tau\) is exactly the squared Wasserstein-2 distance between the estimated and true conditional distributions. The function approximation error in quantile space has a direct interpretation as a distributional distance. No other representation of distributions (densities, CDFs, moment sequences) enjoys such a clean connection to optimal transport. It means that improving the network’s approximation of \(G^*\) — in the ordinary \(L^2\) sense — directly improves the distributional accuracy as measured by the most natural metric on probability distributions.
CRPS as a Wasserstein loss. The Wasserstein distance gives us a way to measure how close two distributions are, but we need a practical loss function that we can minimize during training. The connection is provided by the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), a strictly proper scoring rule for evaluating probabilistic forecasts (Gneiting and Raftery 2007). “Strictly proper” means that the expected score is uniquely minimized when the predictive distribution equals the true data-generating distribution — there is no incentive to hedge or misreport. For a predictive distribution \(F\) and an observation \(y\), the CRPS is defined as \[
\mathrm{CRPS}(F, y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left(F(z) - \mathbf{1}(z \geq y)\right)^2 dz.
\] It can be shown that the CRPS admits the following equivalent representation in terms of quantile functions: \[
\mathrm{CRPS}(F, y) = \int_0^1 2\,\rho_\tau\!\left(y - F^{-1}(\tau)\right) d\tau,
\tag{4.9}\] where \(\rho_\tau(u) = u(\tau - \mathbf{1}(u < 0))\) is the check (pinball) loss from quantile regression.
Furthermore, the CRPS admits a decomposition into forecast accuracy and sharpness. The complete identity from Gneiting and Raftery (2007) is: \[
\mathrm{CRPS}(F, y) = \mathbb{E}_F|X - y| - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_F|X - X'|,
\] where \(X, X' \sim F\) independently. The first term measures the forecast’s expected distance from the observation; the second, \(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_F|X - X'|\), is the sharpness of \(F\) — it measures the spread of the predictive distribution and rewards concentrated forecasts. Taking expectations over \(Y \sim G\) (the true distribution), the expected CRPS relates to the 1-Wasserstein distance: when \(F\) equals \(G\), the CRPS reduces to \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_G|Y - Y'|\), and the excess CRPS from using \(F \neq G\) is controlled by \(W_1(F, G)\). The CRPS is, up to this sharpness correction, the Wasserstein-1 distance between the predictive and true distributions (see Corollary A.1 in Section A.2 for the precise statement). This is why minimizing the pinball loss — which is the integrand in Eq. 4.9 — is a natural training objective for quantile neural networks. Each quantile level \(\tau\) contributes to the overall CRPS, and minimizing the expected pinball loss over random \(\tau\) amounts to minimizing the Wasserstein distance to the true conditional distribution. In practice, the IQN training procedure (described in Chapter 5) samples random quantile levels \(\tau \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) at each training step and minimizes the corresponding pinball loss. This stochastic approximation to the CRPS integral converges to the true CRPS as training progresses, which means that the learned quantile function \(\hat{G}\) converges to the true \(G^*\) in the Wasserstein sense.
This connection closes the loop. The four pillars of the GBC framework that this chapter has established are: First, the noise outsourcing theorem guarantees existence of \(G^*(\tau, x)\) — the conditional quantile function that encodes the full conditional distribution. Second, \(G^*\) is the optimal transport map from \(\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) to \(F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)\), which gives it a geometric interpretation as the most efficient way to reshape uniform noise into the target distribution. Third, the CRPS and its pinball loss integrand provide a natural training objective that measures the Wasserstein distance between our learned \(\hat{G}\) and the truth \(G^*\). Fourth, the universal approximation theorem guarantees that neural networks can approximate \(G^*\) to arbitrary accuracy on compact domains. These four results — existence, optimality, loss function, and approximability — form the theoretical foundation on which the entire GBC framework rests.
In Chapter 5, we turn these ideas into a concrete algorithm.

title: 4  The Noise Outsourcing Theorem
text:
4.10 Summary
The noise outsourcing theorem (Theorem 4.1) tells us that any conditional distribution \(F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)\) can be represented as a deterministic function \(G^*(\tau, x)\) of a uniform random variable \(\tau\) and the conditioning variable \(x\). This function is the conditional quantile function, and it encodes the entire conditional distribution without loss of information.
We then extended the result in three important directions. The multivariate extension (Theorem 4.2) showed that joint distributions over \(d\)-dimensional vectors can be handled through an autoregressive decomposition, where each component is generated by its own quantile function conditioning on all previously generated components. The Bayesian corollary (Corollary 4.1) showed how to apply noise outsourcing to posterior inference, replacing the data-parameter roles and enabling posterior sampling via a single forward pass through a learned network. The optimal transport connection (Proposition 4.3) revealed that the quantile function is not just a map from uniform noise to the target distribution, but the optimal such map in the Wasserstein-2 sense, and that the CRPS training loss directly measures the Wasserstein distance between the learned and true distributions.
Along the way, we established the universality of the approach (Proposition 4.2): neural networks can approximate \(G^*\) to arbitrary accuracy, regardless of the distribution family. We demonstrated this universality with worked examples spanning continuous (Gaussian), discrete (zero-inflated Poisson), and bimodal (mixture) distributions. We also compared the noise outsourcing representation with VAEs and normalizing flows, highlighting the advantages of the fixed-uniform-latent approach: no KL divergence, no posterior collapse, and direct access to quantiles by construction.
The reader may notice a recurring theme: at every turn, the quantile function emerges as the natural object to work with. It is the noise outsourcing map, the optimal transport map, the sufficient representation of the conditional distribution, and the function whose \(L^2\) error equals the Wasserstein distance to the truth. This is not a coincidence — it reflects the deep connection between quantile functions and the geometry of probability distributions. In one dimension, quantile functions are the geometry of distributions, and the GBC framework is built squarely on this insight.
The stage is now set for Chapter 5, where we turn the noise outsourcing theorem into a practical algorithm. The theorem tells us what to learn (the conditional quantile function \(G^*\)); the next chapter will tell us how to learn it using the Implicit Quantile Network architecture.

title: 4  The Noise Outsourcing Theorem
text:
4.11 Exercises
The exercises below are designed to build facility with the noise outsourcing theorem and its connections to optimal transport, sufficient statistics, and generative modeling. Exercises 4.1–4.4 develop core theoretical skills, while Exercises 4.5–4.8 explore the multivariate extension, discrete distributions, the comparison with VAEs, and the connection to Kolmogorov’s representation theorem. We recommend that readers new to quantile functions start with Exercises 4.1 and 4.2, which provide hands-on practice with the noise outsourcing construction for familiar distributions.

Exercise 4.1 Noise outsourcing for the Gaussian model. Consider \(Y \mid X = x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu(x), \sigma^2(x))\) where \(\mu(x) = x^2\) and \(\sigma(x) = e^{x/2}\).

Derive the noise outsourcing map \(G^*(\tau, x) = F_{Y|X}^{-1}(\tau \mid x)\) explicitly.
Verify that for \(U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) independent of \(X\), the random variable \(G^*(U, X)\) has the same conditional distribution as \(Y \mid X\).
Show that \(G^*(\tau, x)\) is monotone increasing in \(\tau\) for every fixed \(x\).
Compute the conditional median (\(\tau = 0.5\)) and the interquartile range (\(\tau = 0.75\) minus \(\tau = 0.25\)) as functions of \(x\).



Exercise 4.2 Quantile function for a Gaussian mixture. Consider \(Y \mid X = x \sim \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(-2, 1) + \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(2, 1)\) (the distribution does not depend on \(x\) in this exercise).

Write down the CDF \(F_Y(y)\) as a mixture of normal CDFs.
Argue that the quantile function \(G^*(\tau) = F_Y^{-1}(\tau)\) cannot be written in closed form.
Using Python (e.g., scipy.optimize.brentq), numerically compute and plot \(G^*(\tau)\) for \(\tau \in (0.01, 0.99)\). Describe the shape of the curve and explain how it reflects the bimodality.
Generate 10,000 samples using \(Y = G^*(U)\) with \(U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) and verify the histogram matches the true density.



Exercise 4.3 Wasserstein distance via quantile functions. Let \(F = \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) and \(G = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\).

Compute \(F^{-1}(\tau) = \Phi^{-1}(\tau)\) and \(G^{-1}(\tau) = \mu + \sigma\Phi^{-1}(\tau)\).
Show that the squared Wasserstein-2 distance is \[
W_2^2(F, G) = \int_0^1 |\Phi^{-1}(\tau) - \mu - \sigma\Phi^{-1}(\tau)|^2 \, d\tau = (\sigma - 1)^2 + \mu^2.
\] Hint: Expand the square as \(|(1-\sigma)\Phi^{-1}(\tau) - \mu|^2 = (1-\sigma)^2[\Phi^{-1}(\tau)]^2 - 2\mu(1-\sigma)\Phi^{-1}(\tau) + \mu^2\). Integrate term by term using \(\int_0^1 [\Phi^{-1}(\tau)]^2 \, d\tau = 1\) (the variance of a standard normal) and \(\int_0^1 \Phi^{-1}(\tau) \, d\tau = \mathbb{E}[Z] = 0\) for \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). The cross term \(-2\mu(1-\sigma)\int_0^1\Phi^{-1}(\tau)\,d\tau\) vanishes because \(\int_0^1\Phi^{-1}(\tau)\,d\tau = \mathbb{E}[Z] = 0\), leaving \((1-\sigma)^2 + \mu^2 = (\sigma-1)^2 + \mu^2\).
Interpret the formula: what does each term measure geometrically?
Compute \(W_1(F, G)\) for the same pair of distributions by evaluating \(\int_0^1 |\Phi^{-1}(\tau) - \mu - \sigma\Phi^{-1}(\tau)| \, d\tau\) numerically for \(\mu = 1\), \(\sigma = 2\).



Exercise 4.4 Monotonicity of the quantile function. Let \(F_{Y|X}(\cdot | x)\) be a conditional CDF for some joint distribution \((X, Y)\).

Prove that the quantile function \(G^*(\tau, x) = \inf\{y : F_{Y|X}(y | x) \geq \tau\}\) is non-decreasing in \(\tau\) for every fixed \(x\). Hint: If \(\tau_1 < \tau_2\), the set \(\{y : F(y) \geq \tau_2\}\) is a subset of \(\{y : F(y) \geq \tau_1\}\).
Give an example where \(G^*(\cdot, x)\) is strictly increasing (i.e., continuous distribution).
Give an example where \(G^*(\cdot, x)\) has flat regions (i.e., distribution with atoms).
Why is monotonicity in \(\tau\) important for the GBC framework? What would go wrong if a learned \(\hat{G}(\tau, x)\) violated monotonicity? Hint: Think about what it means for the “predictive CDF” to be non-decreasing.



Exercise 4.5 Autoregressive noise outsourcing for bivariate normal. Let \((\theta_1, \theta_2) \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 \\ \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2 \end{pmatrix}\right)\).

Write down \(G_1^*(\tau_1, y) = F_{\theta_1|y}^{-1}(\tau_1)\) for the marginal of \(\theta_1\).
Derive the conditional distribution \(\theta_2 \mid \theta_1, y\) and write down \(G_2^*(\tau_2, y, \theta_1) = F_{\theta_2|\theta_1,y}^{-1}(\tau_2)\).
Verify that drawing \(\tau_1, \tau_2 \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) and computing \(\theta_1 = G_1^*(\tau_1, y)\), \(\theta_2 = G_2^*(\tau_2, y, \theta_1)\) produces draws from the correct bivariate normal. Hint: Check that the marginal and conditional distributions match.
Implement this in Python for \(\mu_1 = 1, \mu_2 = 2, \sigma_1 = 1, \sigma_2 = 1.5, \rho = 0.7\). Generate 5000 samples and plot the resulting scatter plot alongside the true density contours.



Exercise 4.6 Noise outsourcing for the zero-inflated Poisson. Consider the zero-inflated Poisson model \(Y \sim \mathrm{ZIP}(\pi_0, \lambda)\) with \(\pi_0 = 0.4\) and \(\lambda = 3\).

Compute \(P(Y = 0)\), \(P(Y = 1)\), \(P(Y = 2)\), and \(P(Y = 3)\) explicitly.
Write down the generalized quantile function \(G^*(\tau)\) as a step function, specifying the breakpoints.
What fraction of the \(\tau\)-axis is mapped to \(Y = 0\)? Explain why this fraction exceeds \(e^{-\lambda}\), the probability of zero under a pure Poisson.
If we train a neural network \(\hat{G}(\tau)\) that produces continuous output, it cannot exactly represent the step function \(G^*\). Discuss how this approximation affects the generated samples. Would rounding the output help?



Exercise 4.7 Noise outsourcing versus VAE. Consider learning the distribution \(Y \sim 0.5 \cdot \mathcal{N}(-3, 0.5^2) + 0.5 \cdot \mathcal{N}(3, 0.5^2)\).

A VAE with a 1D latent space \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and decoder \(Y = \mu_\psi(Z) + \sigma_\psi(Z) \cdot \epsilon\), \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), is trained to maximize the ELBO. Explain why the KL term \(D_{\text{KL}}(q_\phi(z|y) \| \mathcal{N}(0,1))\) creates tension with accurately modeling the bimodal distribution.
Write down the noise outsourcing map \(G^*(\tau)\) for this mixture (you may express it using numerical inversion). Does it suffer from the same tension?
Plot the quantile function \(G^*(\tau)\) and describe its shape. Identify the steep region and explain its probabilistic meaning.
Argue that the noise outsourcing representation cannot suffer from “posterior collapse” (the pathology where the VAE encoder ignores the input). What structural feature of the representation prevents this?



Exercise 4.8 Kolmogorov’s superposition and quantile functions. Kolmogorov’s superposition theorem says any continuous \(f : [0,1]^d \to \mathbb{R}\) can be written as \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_d) = \sum_{j=0}^{2d} \Psi_j(\sum_{i=1}^d \phi_{ij}(x_i))\).

Compare this to the autoregressive noise outsourcing decomposition in Eq. 4.5. Both reduce multivariate functions to compositions of univariate functions. What is the key structural difference?
Kolmogorov’s theorem requires \(2d + 1\) outer functions \(\Psi_j\). The autoregressive decomposition requires \(d\) quantile functions \(G_j^*\). Why does the autoregressive approach need fewer functions? Hint: Think about what additional structure the quantile functions have (monotonicity, probabilistic interpretation) that Kolmogorov’s functions lack.
Modern neural networks are sometimes called “Kolmogorov–Arnold networks” (KANs). Discuss why the IQN architecture, which learns quantile functions, may be better suited to distributional estimation than a generic KAN.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
5.1 Cosine Embedding of \(\tau\)
In the previous chapters, we established the theoretical foundations of quantile functions (Chapter 3) and the noise outsourcing theorem (Chapter 4), which guarantees that any conditional distribution \(Y \mid X\) can be represented as \(Y = G^*(U, X)\) where \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). The natural question is: how do we learn this function \(G^*\) from data?
The answer is the Implicit Quantile Network (IQN), introduced by Dabney et al. (2018) in the context of distributional reinforcement learning and adopted here as the core computational engine of Generative Bayesian Computation. An IQN is a neural network that takes a covariate \(x\) and a quantile level \(\tau \in (0,1)\) and outputs an estimate of the \(\tau\)th conditional quantile: \[
\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x) \approx F^{-1}_{Y \mid X=x}(\tau).
\tag{5.1}\]
What makes IQN “implicit” is that \(\tau\) is treated as a continuous input rather than a fixed grid. We do not pre-specify which quantiles to learn — instead, we sample \(\tau\) uniformly during training and the network learns the entire quantile function simultaneously. This is a departure from classical quantile regression (Koenker 2005), where one fits a separate model for each quantile level.
The chapter is organized as follows. We begin with the cosine embedding that transforms the scalar \(\tau\) into a rich feature vector (Section 5.1). We then describe the full architecture and the three strategies for merging \(\tau\) with \(x\) (Section 5.2). The composite loss function follows (Section 5.3), including a comparison with the Huber quantile loss (Section 5.3.1). Training details appear in Section 5.4, followed by diagnostics for validating a trained IQN (Section 5.5) and a hyperparameter sensitivity study (Section 5.6). We present two worked examples — the motorcycle crash dataset (Section 5.7) and the Friedman function with heteroscedastic noise (Section 5.8) — before closing with exercises (Section 5.9).
The IQN encodes the quantile level \(\tau\) in a specific way. A naive approach would concatenate \(\tau\) as a scalar feature alongside \(x\). This works but is inefficient: the network must learn the entire dependence of \(\hat{Q}\) on \(\tau\) from a one-dimensional input, which is a heavy burden on a few initial weights.
A better approach is to lift \(\tau\) into a higher-dimensional space using a cosine embedding. The idea comes from Fourier analysis: smooth functions on \([0,1]\) are well-approximated by cosine series. Since the quantile function \(F^{-1}(\tau \mid x)\) is typically smooth in \(\tau\) (for a fixed \(x\)), a cosine basis is a natural representation.
The typical choice is \(M = 64\). Each component \(\cos(\pi \tau \cdot i)\) oscillates \(i\) times over \((0,1)\), so the embedding captures both low-frequency trends (small \(i\)) and high-frequency detail (large \(i\)) in the quantile function. The subsequent linear layer and ReLU learn a task-specific combination of these frequencies.
Why cosine and not sine? The cosine basis \(\{\cos(\pi i \tau)\}_{i=0}^{M-1}\) forms an orthonormal system on \([0,1]\) with respect to the standard inner product — it is the Type-II discrete cosine transform basis. This is the same basis used in JPEG compression and has well-known approximation-theoretic properties. Barron (1993) showed that superpositions of such basis functions achieve approximation rates of \(O(N^{-1/2})\) for functions with bounded first moments of the Fourier magnitude distribution, independent of the input dimension.
The following code implements the cosine embedding.
Show code (22 lines)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np

class CosineEmbedding(nn.Module):
    """Cosine embedding for quantile level tau."""
    def __init__(self, M=64, d=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.M = M
        self.fc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(M, d), nn.ReLU())

    def forward(self, tau):
        # tau: scalar or (batch,) tensor
        i = torch.arange(1, self.M + 1, dtype=torch.float32)
        # cos(pi * tau * i) for i = 1, 2, ..., M  (1-indexed per Dabney et al. 2018)
        cos_features = torch.cos(torch.pi * tau * i)  # (M,) or (batch, M)
        return self.fc(cos_features)

# Quick test: embed tau = 0.5
embed = CosineEmbedding(M=64, d=256)
h = embed(torch.tensor(0.5))
print(f"Input: tau = 0.5  ->  Embedding shape: {h.shape}")
To visualize the raw cosine features before the learned linear layer, consider the following plot.
Show code (12 lines)


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

tau_grid = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(6, 3))
for i in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]:
    ax.plot(tau_grid, np.cos(np.pi * tau_grid * i), label=f"i = {i}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\tau$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\cos(\pi \tau \cdot i)$")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Cosine basis functions")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Figure 5.1: Raw cosine embedding features for selected frequencies. Low-frequency components (i=1,2) capture the broad shape of the quantile function, while higher frequencies (i=8,16) add fine-grained detail.
An alternative is a linear embedding, where \(\tau\) is simply passed through a linear layer: \(\phi_{\text{lin}}(\tau) = \text{ReLU}(w \cdot \tau + b)\). This works for simple problems but struggles with non-monotone or rapidly varying quantile functions. The cosine embedding provides a richer starting representation, allowing the network to converge faster and generalize better. We compare the two in Section 5.9.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
TipDefinition 5.1: Cosine Embedding



For \(\tau \in (0,1)\) and embedding dimension \(M\), the cosine embedding is \[
\varphi(\tau) = \bigl(\cos(\pi \tau \cdot 1),\; \cos(\pi \tau \cdot 2),\; \ldots,\; \cos(\pi \tau \cdot M)\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^M.
\tag{5.2}\] This 1-indexed convention follows Dabney et al. (2018) and avoids a constant first feature (\(\cos(\pi\tau\cdot 0)=1\) for all \(\tau\)), which carries no information about \(\tau\).
The embedded vector is then passed through a learned linear layer followed by ReLU: \[
\phi(\tau) = \text{ReLU}\bigl(W_\tau \, \varphi(\tau) + b_\tau\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^d,
\tag{5.3}\] where \(W_\tau \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times M}\) and \(b_\tau \in \mathbb{R}^d\) are learnable parameters. This differs slightly from Dabney et al. (2018), who apply ReLU elementwise to each cosine feature before the linear layer; our formulation applies ReLU after the linear transform, which is more expressive as the linear layer can mix frequencies before the nonlinearity.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
5.2 Architecture
We can now describe the full IQN architecture. The network takes two inputs — the covariate \(x \in \mathbb{R}^p\) and the quantile level \(\tau \in (0,1)\) — and outputs a scalar estimate \(\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x) \in \mathbb{R}\).
The architecture has four stages. A covariate encoder MLP maps \(x\) to a hidden representation \(h_x \in \mathbb{R}^d\), while the cosine embedding maps \(\tau\) to \(h_\tau \in \mathbb{R}^d\) of the same dimension. These are merged via the element-wise product \(h = h_x \odot h_\tau\), and further MLP layers in the output head then map \(h\) to the scalar output.
The multiplicative interaction lets \(\tau\) modulate the feature representation of \(x\), rather than merely being concatenated. The covariate encoder learns which features of \(x\) are relevant, and the quantile encoder gates these features depending on which part of the distribution we are querying. This is far more expressive than additive combination.






TipDefinition 5.2: IQN Architecture



The IQN maps \((x, \tau)\) to \(\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x)\) via \[
\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x) = g_\theta\bigl(\psi_\theta(x) \odot \phi_\theta(\tau)\bigr),
\tag{5.4}\] where \(\psi_\theta : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^d\) is the covariate encoder, \(\phi_\theta : (0,1) \to \mathbb{R}^d\) is the cosine-based quantile encoder, \(\odot\) denotes element-wise multiplication, and \(g_\theta : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) is the output head.


A schematic of the architecture:





flowchart TD
    X["Input x ∈ ℝᵖ"] --> EX["ψ: Linear + ReLU"]
    T["Input τ ∈ (0,1)"] --> COS["cos(πτ·i), i=1…M\n(M=64 frequencies)"]
    COS --> ET["Linear + ReLU"]
    EX --> HX["h_x ∈ ℝᵈ"]
    ET --> HT["h_τ ∈ ℝᵈ"]
    HX --> MUL["⊙  element-wise multiply"]
    HT --> MUL
    MUL --> G1["Linear + ReLU"]
    G1 --> G2["Linear + Tanh"]
    G2 --> G3["Linear → ℝ"]
    G3 --> OUT["Q̂(τ | x)"]







5.2.1 Multiplicative vs. Additive vs. Concatenation Merging
There are three natural ways to combine the hidden representations \(h_x \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(h_\tau \in \mathbb{R}^d\) before passing them to the output head. Each has a distinct inductive bias, and the choice matters for both expressiveness and training stability.
The multiplicative merge computes \(h = h_x \odot h_\tau\), where \(\odot\) denotes element-wise (Hadamard) product. This is the strategy used by Dabney et al. (2018) and is our default throughout this book. In the multiplicative scheme, each component of \(h_\tau\) acts as a gate on the corresponding component of \(h_x\). When \(h_\tau^{(j)} \approx 0\), the \(j\)th feature of \(x\) is suppressed for that quantile level; when \(h_\tau^{(j)} \approx 1\), it passes through unchanged. This gating mechanism is the same one that drives the success of attention and gating architectures more broadly. For quantile estimation, it allows the network to select different features for different parts of the distribution — the features that matter for the 5th percentile may differ from those that matter for the 95th percentile, and the multiplicative merge handles this naturally.
The additive merge computes \(h = h_x + h_\tau\). This is simpler and has a clear interpretation: the quantile level shifts the covariate representation by a fixed offset. The additive merge works well when the quantile function has a location-scale structure \(Q(\tau \mid x) = \mu(x) + \sigma(x) \cdot \Phi^{-1}(\tau)\), because the offset can capture the \(\Phi^{-1}(\tau)\) term. However, it struggles when different quantile levels require qualitatively different feature representations, because the same offset is added to every component of \(h_x\) regardless of whether that component is relevant for the current quantile level. On the motorcycle data, we observe that the additive merge tends to produce slightly wider prediction intervals in the low-variance region (\(t < 15\) ms) because it cannot selectively suppress features the way the multiplicative merge can.
The concatenation merge computes \(h = [h_x; h_\tau] \in \mathbb{R}^{2d}\), simply stacking the two vectors. This is the most general approach — it places no structural constraint on how \(\tau\) and \(x\) interact — but it doubles the dimension of the input to the output head, increasing the parameter count. In principle, concatenation can represent any function of \((h_x, h_\tau)\), including both multiplicative and additive interactions, but in practice it requires more data and more training epochs to learn these interactions from scratch. On small datasets like the motorcycle data (\(n = 133\)), concatenation tends to overfit and produce noisy quantile estimates. On larger datasets (\(n > 5{,}000\)), it performs comparably to the multiplicative merge but with roughly twice the parameters.
We recommend the multiplicative merge as the default for two reasons. First, the gating mechanism provides a strong inductive bias that the quantile level should modulate (rather than merely shift) the feature representation. Second, it keeps the parameter count the same as the additive merge while being substantially more expressive. The additive merge is a reasonable fallback for very simple problems where the distribution is approximately location-scale.
Here is the full implementation.


Show code (51 lines)

class IQN(nn.Module):
    """Implicit Quantile Network.

    Args:
        xdim: dimension of input covariates
        hdim: hidden layer dimension (default 256)
        M: number of cosine embedding frequencies (default 64)
    """
    def __init__(self, xdim, hdim=256, M=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.M = M
        # Quantile encoder: cosine embedding -> linear -> ReLU
        self.fc_tau = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(M, hdim), nn.ReLU())
        # Covariate encoder: linear -> ReLU
        self.fc_x = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(xdim, hdim), nn.ReLU())
        # Output head after multiplicative merge
        self.head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hdim, hdim), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hdim, 64),   nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 1)
        )
        self._init_weights()

    def _init_weights(self):
        for m in self.modules():
            if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.xavier_uniform_(m.weight)
                nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)

    def forward(self, x, tau):
        """
        Args:
            x:   (batch, xdim) covariate tensor
            tau: scalar float in (0, 1)
        Returns:
            (batch, 1) predicted quantile values
        """
        i = torch.arange(1, self.M + 1, dtype=torch.float32)
        h_tau = self.fc_tau(torch.cos(i * torch.pi * tau))  # (hdim,), i=1..M
        h_x = self.fc_x(x)                                  # (batch, hdim)
        h = h_x * h_tau.unsqueeze(0)                         # (batch, hdim)
        return self.head(h)                                  # (batch, 1)

# Verify dimensions
model = IQN(xdim=2, hdim=256, M=64)
x_test = torch.randn(32, 2)
q_hat = model(x_test, 0.5)
print(f"Input: x.shape = {x_test.shape}, tau = 0.5")
print(f"Output: Q_hat.shape = {q_hat.shape}")
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Total parameters: {n_params:,}")


We use \(d = 256\) throughout: for very low-dimensional problems (\(p \leq 3\)), \(d = 128\) suffices, while high-dimensional inputs may benefit from \(d = 512\). Three hidden layers—one in each encoder plus one in the output head—is our default, with deeper networks helping for complex functions at the cost of more training epochs. The activation choices are ReLU in the encoders, Tanh in the penultimate layer (to bound intermediate representations), and no activation on the final output since quantiles are unbounded. For \(p = 2\), the model has roughly 135K parameters—modest by modern standards but sufficient for the problems in this book.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
5.3 The Three-Term Loss
Training the IQN requires a loss function that encourages the output \(\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x)\) to match the true conditional quantile \(F^{-1}_{Y|X}(\tau)\). The natural choice is the pinball loss \(\rho_\tau\) from Eq. 3.2, where \(\rho_\tau(u) = \max(\tau u, (\tau-1)u)\) and \(u = y - \hat{Q}(\tau \mid x)\) is the residual.
A proper scoring rule is a loss function that is uniquely minimized when the predicted distribution equals the true conditional distribution. A loss that is not strictly proper can be “gamed” — a miscalibrated forecast may achieve a lower loss than the truth. Minimizing the expected pinball loss over \(\tau\) yields the CRPS — the continuous ranked probability score — which is a strictly proper scoring rule (Gneiting and Raftery 2007): \[
\text{CRPS}(F, y) = 2\int_0^1 \rho_\tau\bigl(y - F^{-1}(\tau)\bigr) \, d\tau.
\tag{5.5}\]
By sampling \(\tau\) uniformly during training and minimizing the pinball loss, the IQN is implicitly minimizing the CRPS. This means the IQN’s training objective is a strictly proper scoring rule, and the network has no incentive to produce miscalibrated predictions. The convergence is not instantaneous — finite training introduces estimation error — but the direction is correct.
In the GBC framework, we use a composite loss that combines three terms.






TipDefinition 5.3: GBC Composite Loss



For a training pair \((x, y)\) and a sampled quantile level \(\tau \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\), the GBC composite loss is \[
\mathcal{L}(x, y, \tau; \theta) = w_1 \cdot L_{\text{pinball}} + w_2 \cdot L_{\text{CRPS}} + w_3 \cdot L_{\text{MAE}},
\tag{5.6}\] where \(L_{\text{pinball}} = \rho_\tau(y - \hat{Q}(\tau \mid x))\) is the standard pinball loss, \(L_{\text{CRPS}}\) is estimated by averaging the pinball loss over multiple sampled \(\tau\) values, and \(L_{\text{MAE}} = |y - \hat{\mu}(x)|\) is the mean absolute error of a location anchor. Default weights: \((w_1, w_2, w_3) = (0.70, 0.20, 0.10)\).


Each term plays a distinct role. The pinball loss (\(w_1\)) is the primary driver: at each training step, we sample a fresh \(\tau\) and compute the asymmetric pinball penalty, so over many steps the network sees all quantile levels uniformly and implicitly optimizes the CRPS. The CRPS term (\(w_2\)) adds an explicit regularizer by sampling a small batch of \(\tau\) values (say 16) and averaging their pinball losses, reducing gradient variance compared to using a single \(\tau\) per step. The MAE anchor (\(w_3\)) keeps the median prediction well-calibrated: without it, the network may produce accurate tail quantiles but a poor point forecast, so this term encourages \(\hat{Q}(0.5 \mid x) \approx \text{median}(Y \mid X=x)\).
The weights \((0.70, 0.20, 0.10)\) work well as a default across most settings, including problems with jump discontinuities (Chapter 8), where the pinball-dominant weighting avoids having the MAE anchor pull predictions toward a blended mean near the jump boundary. For smooth, well-behaved functions, equal weights \((0.33, 0.33, 0.34)\) also work well.
The implementation also includes a monotonicity regularizer. Since the quantile function must be non-decreasing in \(\tau\), we penalize crossings: if \(\tau < 0.5\), we penalize cases where the prediction is too high (relative to the median); if \(\tau > 0.5\), we penalize cases where it is too low. This is encoded implicitly in the original IQN loss through the asymmetric monotonicity term.


Show code (47 lines)

def pinball_loss(y, q_hat, tau):
    """Pinball (quantile) loss.

    Args:
        y:     (batch,) true values
        q_hat: (batch,) predicted quantiles
        tau:   float in (0, 1)
    Returns:
        scalar loss
    """
    e = y - q_hat
    return torch.mean(torch.maximum(tau * e, (tau - 1) * e))


def composite_loss(model, x, y, weights=(0.70, 0.20, 0.10)):
    """GBC three-term composite loss.

    Samples tau ~ Uniform(0,1) at each call.
    """
    w1, w2, w3 = weights
    tau = torch.rand(1).item()

    # Term 1: Pinball loss at sampled tau
    q_hat = model(x, tau).squeeze(-1)
    L_pinball = pinball_loss(y, q_hat, tau)

    # Term 2: CRPS estimate (average pinball over 16 tau values)
    crps_taus = torch.rand(16)
    L_crps = 0.0
    for t in crps_taus:
        q_t = model(x, t.item()).squeeze(-1)
        L_crps = L_crps + pinball_loss(y, q_t, t.item())
    L_crps = L_crps / len(crps_taus)

    # Term 3: MAE at median (location anchor)
    q_median = model(x, 0.5).squeeze(-1)
    L_mae = torch.mean(torch.abs(y - q_median))

    return w1 * L_pinball + w2 * L_crps + w3 * L_mae


# Quick check
model = IQN(xdim=1, hdim=64, M=32)
x_demo = torch.randn(16, 1)
y_demo = torch.randn(16)
loss_val = composite_loss(model, x_demo, y_demo)
print(f"Composite loss value: {loss_val.item():.4f}")








Note



Remark. The loss function above samples \(\tau\) independently at each training step. Over the course of training with thousands of steps, every quantile level is visited many times. This is the “implicit” nature of IQN: the network never commits to a fixed grid of quantiles, yet it learns the entire quantile function. Dabney et al. (2018) showed that this uniform sampling strategy is statistically efficient in the sense that the resulting estimator converges to the true conditional quantile function under mild regularity conditions.



5.3.1 Huber Quantile Loss
The pinball loss \(\rho_\tau(u)\) is piecewise linear and therefore non-smooth at \(u = 0\). While stochastic gradient descent handles non-smooth objectives perfectly well in practice, there is a smooth alternative: the Huber quantile loss, which replaces the kink at zero with a quadratic bowl.
The motivation for smoothing is the same as in standard regression: when the residuals are close to zero, the gradient of the pinball loss jumps discontinuously from \(\tau - 1\) to \(\tau\). This can cause oscillation in the optimization trajectory, particularly in the late stages of training when the network is close to the optimum and small gradient perturbations matter. The Huber quantile loss eliminates this jump by interpolating quadratically within a narrow band \(|u| \leq \kappa\).






TipDefinition 5.4: Huber Quantile Loss



For a threshold \(\kappa > 0\) and quantile level \(\tau \in (0,1)\), the Huber quantile loss is \[
\rho_\tau^\kappa(u) = \begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2\kappa} u^2 \cdot |\tau - \mathbf{1}_{u < 0}| & \text{if } |u| \leq \kappa, \\
\rho_\tau(u) - \frac{\kappa}{2} \cdot |\tau - \mathbf{1}_{u < 0}| & \text{if } |u| > \kappa.
\end{cases}
\tag{5.7}\] The parameter \(\kappa\) controls the width of the quadratic zone. As \(\kappa \to 0\), we recover the standard pinball loss.


When does the Huber variant help? In our experience, the answer is: rarely for the IQN. The standard pinball loss works well because the stochastic gradient from sampling \(\tau\) already introduces enough noise to smooth the optimization landscape. The Huber variant can help when training on data with very heavy tails, where large residuals dominate the gradient and the quadratic damping near zero helps the network focus on getting the bulk of the distribution right before fine-tuning the tails. On the motorcycle data, switching from pinball to Huber quantile loss (\(\kappa = 1.0\)) makes no measurable difference in CRPS (both achieve approximately 12.5 averaged over 50 train/test splits). On a synthetic heavy-tailed example with \(t_3\) errors, the Huber variant reduces CRPS by about 3–5%, a modest improvement. We use the standard pinball loss throughout this book unless otherwise noted.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
5.4 Training Details
Training an IQN follows standard deep learning practice with a few GBC-specific choices. We use Adam with learning rate \(\eta_0 = 10^{-3}\) and weight decay \(10^{-4}\), together with cosine annealing from \(\eta_0\) to \(\eta_{\min} = 10^{-5}\) over \(T\) epochs. Batch sizes of 256 or 512 work well in practice, with 3000 epochs for standard problems and 5000–8000 for complex surfaces. We monitor validation CRPS for early stopping, halting if no improvement is seen for 500 epochs.
The cosine annealing schedule is important. It starts with a high learning rate for rapid exploration, then gradually reduces it to fine-tune the quantile estimates: \[
\eta_t = \eta_{\min} + \frac{1}{2}(\eta_0 - \eta_{\min})\left(1 + \cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{T}\right)\right).
\tag{5.8}\]
This schedule outperforms both fixed learning rates and step-decay schedules in our experiments, particularly for the tail quantiles where precise calibration matters.
Data normalization. We always standardize both inputs and outputs before training: \[
\tilde{x} = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s_x}, \quad \tilde{y} = \frac{y - \bar{y}}{s_y},
\] where \(\bar{x}, s_x\) and \(\bar{y}, s_y\) are the training-set means and standard deviations. After prediction, we invert the transformation: \(\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x) = s_y \cdot \hat{Q}_{\text{norm}}(\tau \mid \tilde{x}) + \bar{y}\).
Sampling \(\tau\) per mini-batch. At each training step, we sample a single \(\tau \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) and apply it to the entire mini-batch. An alternative is to sample a different \(\tau\) per example, but the shared-\(\tau\) approach has lower variance in practice because the network sees the same quantile level applied consistently across the batch. Over thousands of training steps, all quantile levels are covered uniformly.
Here is the complete training loop.


Show code (72 lines)

def train_iqn(X_train, y_train, epochs=3000, hdim=256, M=64,
              lr=1e-3, wd=1e-4, weights=(0.70, 0.20, 0.10), seed=42):
    """Train an IQN model.

    Args:
        X_train: (n, p) numpy array of covariates
        y_train: (n,) numpy array of responses
        epochs:  number of training epochs
        hdim:    hidden dimension
        M:       cosine embedding dimension
        lr:      initial learning rate
        wd:      weight decay
        weights: (w_pinball, w_crps, w_mae)
        seed:    random seed

    Returns:
        model, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std
    """
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    xdim = X_train.shape[1]

    # Normalize
    x_mean, x_std = X_train.mean(0), X_train.std(0) + 1e-8
    y_mean, y_std = float(y_train.mean()), float(y_train.std()) + 1e-8
    Xt = torch.tensor((X_train - x_mean) / x_std, dtype=torch.float32)
    yt = torch.tensor((y_train - y_mean) / y_std, dtype=torch.float32)

    model = IQN(xdim, hdim=hdim, M=M)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=wd)
    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(
        optimizer, T_max=epochs, eta_min=lr * 0.01
    )

    model.train()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = composite_loss(model, Xt, yt, weights)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        scheduler.step()

    model.eval()
    return model, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std


def predict_quantiles(model, X_test, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std,
                      taus=None, n_tau=500):
    """Predict quantile function at test points.

    Args:
        model:  trained IQN
        X_test: (n_test, p) numpy array
        taus:   specific tau values, or None for uniform grid
        n_tau:  number of tau values if taus is None

    Returns:
        quantiles: (n_tau, n_test) array
        tau_grid:  (n_tau,) array
    """
    if taus is None:
        tau_grid = np.linspace(0.005, 0.995, n_tau)
    else:
        tau_grid = np.array(taus)

    Xt = torch.tensor((X_test - x_mean) / x_std, dtype=torch.float32)
    quantiles = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for tau in tau_grid:
            q = model(Xt, float(tau)).squeeze(-1).numpy()
            quantiles.append(q * y_std + y_mean)

    return np.array(quantiles), tau_grid








Note



Implementation note. The training loop above passes the entire dataset as a single batch. For large datasets (\(n > 10{,}000\)), mini-batch training with a DataLoader is recommended. The gbc package provides gbc.iqn.IQN and gbc.train.fit_iqn with mini-batching, gradient clipping, and checkpointing built in.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
5.5 Diagnostics and Validation
Training an IQN is easy; knowing whether the result is trustworthy requires diagnostics. In this section we develop four checks that every practitioner should run after fitting an IQN: Probability Integral Transform (PIT) histograms, CRPS convergence curves, quantile crossing detection, and out-of-sample coverage analysis. These diagnostics are not unique to IQN — they apply to any distributional forecast — but the IQN makes them particularly easy to compute because the quantile function is available in closed form (a single forward pass).

5.5.1 PIT Histograms
The Probability Integral Transform is the oldest and most fundamental calibration check in statistics. The idea is simple: if \(\hat{F}(\cdot \mid x_i)\) is the predicted CDF at observation \(i\), then the PIT value is \[
u_i = \hat{F}(y_i \mid x_i).
\tag{5.9}\] If the model is perfectly calibrated — meaning \(\hat{F} = F\) where \(F\) is the true conditional CDF — then \(u_1, \ldots, u_n\) are i.i.d. \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\) by the probability integral transform theorem. Deviations from uniformity reveal specific miscalibration patterns: a U-shaped histogram indicates underdispersion (prediction intervals too narrow), an inverted-U indicates overdispersion (intervals too wide), and skew indicates systematic bias.
For the IQN, computing the PIT values requires inverting the quantile function. Given a trained model \(\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x)\), we evaluate on a fine grid of \(\tau\) values and find the level at which the predicted quantile crosses the observed value: \[
\hat{u}_i = \inf\bigl\{\tau \in (0,1) : \hat{Q}(\tau \mid x_i) \geq y_i\bigr\}.
\] In practice, we evaluate \(\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x_i)\) on a grid of 500 \(\tau\) values and use linear interpolation to find the crossing point.


Show code (33 lines)

def compute_pit(model, X, y, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std, n_tau=500):
    """Compute PIT values for a trained IQN.

    Args:
        model:  trained IQN
        X, y:   data arrays
        x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std: normalization params
        n_tau:  grid resolution

    Returns:
        pit_values: (n,) array of PIT values in (0,1)
    """
    quantiles, tau_grid = predict_quantiles(
        model, X, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std, n_tau=n_tau
    )
    n = len(y)
    pit_values = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n):
        # Find tau where Q(tau | x_i) crosses y_i
        idx = np.searchsorted(quantiles[:, i], y[i])
        if idx == 0:
            pit_values[i] = tau_grid[0]
        elif idx >= n_tau:
            pit_values[i] = tau_grid[-1]
        else:
            # Linear interpolation
            frac = (y[i] - quantiles[idx-1, i]) / (
                quantiles[idx, i] - quantiles[idx-1, i] + 1e-10
            )
            pit_values[i] = tau_grid[idx-1] + frac * (
                tau_grid[idx] - tau_grid[idx-1]
            )
    return pit_values




5.5.2 CRPS Convergence
Monitoring the CRPS on a held-out validation set during training serves as a convergence diagnostic. Unlike the training loss — which combines three terms with potentially conflicting gradients — the validation CRPS measures the single quantity we care about: how well the predicted quantile function matches the true conditional distribution on unseen data.
A well-behaved training run shows the validation CRPS decreasing rapidly in the first 500–1000 epochs, then leveling off as the network converges. Warning signs include: the CRPS increasing after an initial decrease (overfitting), the CRPS oscillating wildly (learning rate too high or batch size too small), or the CRPS plateauing at a high value (underfitting, possibly due to insufficient model capacity).


5.5.3 Quantile Crossing Detection
A valid quantile function must be non-decreasing in \(\tau\): for \(\tau_1 < \tau_2\), we require \(\hat{Q}(\tau_1 \mid x) \leq \hat{Q}(\tau_2 \mid x)\) for all \(x\). When this property is violated, the predicted distribution is internally inconsistent. Quantile crossings are rare with the IQN architecture — the cosine embedding and multiplicative merge provide a strong inductive bias toward smoothness in \(\tau\) — but they can occur on small datasets or with poorly tuned hyperparameters.
We detect crossings by evaluating the predicted quantiles on a grid and checking the monotonicity condition. The following function counts the number and severity of crossings.


Show code (18 lines)

def detect_crossings(model, X_test, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std, n_tau=200):
    """Detect quantile crossings in a trained IQN.

    Returns:
        n_crossings: number of (test point, tau pair) violations
        max_violation: largest crossing magnitude
        frac_points: fraction of test points with at least one crossing
    """
    quantiles, tau_grid = predict_quantiles(
        model, X_test, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std, n_tau=n_tau
    )
    # Check monotonicity along tau axis
    diffs = np.diff(quantiles, axis=0)  # (n_tau-1, n_test)
    violations = diffs < 0
    n_crossings = int(violations.sum())
    max_violation = float(-diffs[violations].min()) if n_crossings > 0 else 0.0
    points_with_crossing = (violations.any(axis=0)).mean()
    return n_crossings, max_violation, points_with_crossing




5.5.4 Out-of-Sample Coverage
The ultimate test of a distributional forecast is whether it covers the observed data at the nominal rate. For a nominal level \(1 - \alpha\), we compute the prediction interval \([\hat{Q}(\alpha/2 \mid x_i),\; \hat{Q}(1 - \alpha/2 \mid x_i)]\) and check whether \(y_i\) falls inside. The empirical coverage is the fraction of test points that are covered. A well-calibrated model achieves empirical coverage close to the nominal level across all \(\alpha\).
We compute coverage at several nominal levels and report the results as a coverage table. Systematic undercoverage (empirical \(<\) nominal) indicates the model is overconfident; overcoverage indicates it is too conservative. The IQN on the motorcycle data typically achieves 80–83% empirical coverage at the 90% nominal level (slightly undercovering), which can be improved to 87–88% by ensembling five independently trained models.


Show code (20 lines)

def compute_coverage(model, X, y, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std,
                     nominal_levels=(0.50, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95)):
    """Compute empirical coverage at several nominal levels.

    Returns:
        dict mapping nominal level -> empirical coverage
    """
    quantiles, tau_grid = predict_quantiles(
        model, X, x_mean, x_std, y_mean, y_std, n_tau=500
    )
    coverages = {}
    for level in nominal_levels:
        alpha = 1 - level
        lo_idx = np.argmin(np.abs(tau_grid - alpha / 2))
        hi_idx = np.argmin(np.abs(tau_grid - (1 - alpha / 2)))
        lo = quantiles[lo_idx, :]
        hi = quantiles[hi_idx, :]
        covered = ((y >= lo) & (y <= hi)).mean()
        coverages[level] = float(covered)
    return coverages

The main takeaways from Table 5.1 are as follows. The number of training epochs has the largest effect: too few epochs (1000) leave the model underfit, while 2000–3000 epochs suffice for the motorcycle dataset. The hidden dimension matters moderately: \(d = 64\) is too small for this heteroscedastic problem, while \(d = 128\) and \(d = 256\) perform similarly, suggesting that 128 is a safe minimum for 1D problems. The cosine embedding dimension \(M\) matters least: values from 16 to 64 give nearly identical CRPS, because the motorcycle quantile function is smooth in \(\tau\) and does not require high-frequency detail. For higher-dimensional problems with more complex conditional distributions, larger \(M\) becomes more important.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
5.7 Example: Motorcycle Data
We demonstrate IQN on the classic motorcycle crash dataset (Silverman 1985), which records head acceleration (in \(g\)) versus time (in milliseconds) for \(n = 133\) simulated motorcycle crashes. This dataset is a benchmark for heteroscedastic regression because the variance of the acceleration changes dramatically: small before impact (\(t < 15\) ms), large during the crash event (\(15 < t < 35\) ms), and moderate afterward.


Show code (11 lines)


Code
# The motorcycle dataset (Silverman, 1985) — from R's MASS::mcycle
# Acceleration (g) vs time (ms) for 133 observations
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.scatter(moto_times, moto_accel, s=12, alpha=0.6, color='k', zorder=3)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Acceleration (g)")
ax.set_title("Motorcycle crash data (Silverman, 1985)")
ax.axvspan(15, 35, alpha=0.08, color='red', label='High-variance region')
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Figure 5.2: Motorcycle crash data: head acceleration versus time after impact. The variance increases dramatically during the crash event (15-35 ms).





We now train an IQN on this dataset and visualize the learned quantile fan.


Show code (9 lines)

# Prepare data
X_moto = moto_times.reshape(-1, 1)
y_moto = moto_accel

# Train IQN (small model, 2000 epochs for this demo)
model_moto, xm, xs, ym, ys = train_iqn(
    X_moto, y_moto, epochs=2000, hdim=128, M=32, seed=42
)
print("Training complete.")




Show code (37 lines)


Code
# Predict on a fine grid
X_grid = np.linspace(2, 58, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
quantiles, tau_grid = predict_quantiles(
    model_moto, X_grid, xm, xs, ym, ys, n_tau=200
)

# Extract key quantiles
def get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, level):
    idx = np.argmin(np.abs(tau_grid - level))
    return quantiles[idx, :]

q05  = get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, 0.05)
q10  = get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, 0.10)
q25  = get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, 0.25)
q50  = get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, 0.50)
q75  = get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, 0.75)
q90  = get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, 0.90)
q95  = get_q(quantiles, tau_grid, 0.95)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(7, 4))
x_plot = X_grid.ravel()
# 90% interval
ax.fill_between(x_plot, q05, q95, alpha=0.15, color='steelblue', label='90% PI')
# 80% interval
ax.fill_between(x_plot, q10, q90, alpha=0.20, color='steelblue', label='80% PI')
# 50% interval
ax.fill_between(x_plot, q25, q75, alpha=0.30, color='steelblue', label='50% PI')
# Median
ax.plot(x_plot, q50, color='steelblue', linewidth=2, label='Median')
# Data
ax.scatter(moto_times, moto_accel, s=12, alpha=0.6, color='k', zorder=3)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Acceleration (g)")
ax.set_title("IQN quantile fan — Motorcycle data")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='lower right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Figure 5.3: IQN quantile fan for the motorcycle data. The shaded bands show the 50%, 80%, and 90% prediction intervals. The network correctly captures the heteroscedastic variance structure: narrow bands before impact, wide during the crash, and narrowing again afterward.





Several features are visible in Figure 5.3. The prediction bands are narrow before impact (\(t < 15\) ms), wide during the crash (\(15 < t < 35\) ms), and narrow again as the acceleration returns to zero—the IQN has automatically learned the variance structure without being told anything about it. During the crash, the lower quantiles (\(\tau = 0.05\)) drop more sharply than the upper quantiles rise, reflecting the asymmetric distribution of crash severity. And despite using only 133 training points, the quantile bands are smooth and non-crossing, a consequence of the cosine embedding which imposes a soft smoothness prior in the \(\tau\)-direction.
Compared to a Gaussian process (GP) with a Matern kernel, the IQN has two advantages on this dataset. First, the GP assumes Gaussian conditional distributions, so its prediction bands are always symmetric around the mean. The IQN makes no such assumption and can capture asymmetric tails. Second, the GP must estimate a single noise variance parameter (or a heteroscedastic extension like hetGP), while the IQN directly models the entire conditional distribution.
We can now run the diagnostics developed in Section 5.5 on this fitted model. The PIT histogram and coverage analysis provide a quantitative assessment of calibration quality.


Show code (17 lines)


Code
# Compute PIT values
pit_vals = compute_pit(model_moto, X_moto, y_moto, xm, xs, ym, ys)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(5, 3))
ax.hist(pit_vals, bins=20, density=True, alpha=0.7, color='steelblue',
        edgecolor='white')
ax.axhline(1.0, color='k', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Uniform')
ax.set_xlabel("PIT value")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.set_title("PIT histogram — Motorcycle IQN")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Coverage and crossing diagnostics (used in prose discussion below)
cov = compute_coverage(model_moto, X_moto, y_moto, xm, xs, ym, ys)
nc, mv, fp = detect_crossings(model_moto, X_grid, xm, xs, ym, ys)









Figure 5.4: PIT histogram for the motorcycle IQN. A perfectly calibrated model would produce a uniform histogram (dashed line). The slight excess at the extremes suggests mild underdispersion in the tails.





Figure 5.5 shows the full comparison between GBC (IQN ensemble with \(K = 5\)) and hetGP on the motorcycle data, using 50 random 80:20 train/test splits. The prediction bands from both methods capture the heteroscedastic structure, but the GP’s symmetric Gaussian intervals are visible in the crash region where the true conditional distribution is asymmetric.








Figure 5.5: Motorcycle benchmark: GBC ensemble (\(K = 5\)) vs. hetGP prediction bands across 50 random splits. Both methods capture the heteroscedastic variance structure. GBC achieves CRPS = 12.49 vs. hetGP CRPS = 12.56.

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
section: 5.8 Example: Friedman Function with Heteroscedastic Noise
text:
5.8 Example: Friedman Function with Heteroscedastic Noise
The motorcycle data is one-dimensional and low-noise. To stress-test the IQN on a higher-dimensional problem, we turn to a 1D slice of the Friedman function with heteroscedastic noise. The Friedman function (Friedman 1991) is a standard benchmark in the surrogate modeling literature: \[
f(x) = 10 \sin(\pi x_1 x_2) + 20(x_3 - 0.5)^2 + 10 x_4 + 5 x_5, \quad x \in [0,1]^{10}.
\] Five of the ten input dimensions are active (with a nonlinear interaction between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)), and the remaining five are inert. For this demonstration, we simplify to a 1D version to allow easy visualization while retaining the essential character of the problem: \[
Y = 10\sin(\pi x) + \sigma(x)\,\varepsilon, \quad x \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1), \quad \varepsilon \sim N(0,1),
\] where \(\sigma(x) = 1 + 3x\) introduces heteroscedastic noise that grows with \(x\). The conditional mean is a smooth sinusoidal curve, but the conditional variance increases linearly across the input domain. A good quantile model should produce narrow prediction bands near \(x = 0\) and wide bands near \(x = 1\).


Show code (14 lines)

# Generate Friedman 1D data with heteroscedastic noise
np.random.seed(123)
n_fried = 200
x_fried = np.random.uniform(0, 1, n_fried)
sigma_fried = 1.0 + 3.0 * x_fried
y_fried = 10 * np.sin(np.pi * x_fried) + sigma_fried * np.random.randn(n_fried)

X_fried = x_fried.reshape(-1, 1)

# Train IQN
model_fried, xm_f, xs_f, ym_f, ys_f = train_iqn(
    X_fried, y_fried, epochs=1000, hdim=128, M=32, seed=7
)
print("Friedman model trained.")




Show code (35 lines)


Code
X_grid_f = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
q_fried, tau_f = predict_quantiles(
    model_fried, X_grid_f, xm_f, xs_f, ym_f, ys_f, n_tau=200
)

q05_f = get_q(q_fried, tau_f, 0.05)
q25_f = get_q(q_fried, tau_f, 0.25)
q50_f = get_q(q_fried, tau_f, 0.50)
q75_f = get_q(q_fried, tau_f, 0.75)
q95_f = get_q(q_fried, tau_f, 0.95)

# True mean and quantiles
xg = X_grid_f.ravel()
true_mean = 10 * np.sin(np.pi * xg)
true_sigma = 1.0 + 3.0 * xg
from scipy.stats import norm
true_q05 = true_mean + norm.ppf(0.05) * true_sigma
true_q95 = true_mean + norm.ppf(0.95) * true_sigma

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(x_fried, y_fried, s=6, alpha=0.3, color='gray', zorder=1)
# Predicted bands
ax.fill_between(xg, q05_f, q95_f, alpha=0.15, color='steelblue', label='90% PI (IQN)')
ax.fill_between(xg, q25_f, q75_f, alpha=0.30, color='steelblue', label='50% PI (IQN)')
ax.plot(xg, q50_f, color='steelblue', linewidth=2, label='Median (IQN)')
# True quantiles
ax.plot(xg, true_mean, 'k--', linewidth=1.5, label='True mean')
ax.plot(xg, true_q05, 'r:', linewidth=1, label='True 5%/95%')
ax.plot(xg, true_q95, 'r:', linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_title("IQN quantile fan — Friedman 1D with heteroscedastic noise")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc='upper left')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Figure 5.6: IQN quantile fan for the 1D Friedman function with heteroscedastic noise. The prediction bands widen as x increases, correctly tracking the growing noise variance sigma(x) = 1 + 3x. The true conditional mean (dashed black) is captured by the median prediction.





The results confirm that the IQN captures both the smooth mean function and the changing variance. Near \(x = 0\), where \(\sigma(x) = 1\), the 90% prediction interval is narrow and closely tracks the true 5th and 95th percentiles (red dotted lines). Near \(x = 1\), where \(\sigma(x) = 4\), the bands widen appropriately. The median prediction (solid blue) aligns closely with the true conditional mean (dashed black), demonstrating that the MAE anchor in the composite loss does its job of keeping the point forecast well-calibrated.
This example also illustrates a contrast with classical approaches. A standard linear quantile regression would fit parallel lines for each quantile level, completely missing the curvature of the mean function. A Gaussian process with constant noise would produce symmetric prediction bands of constant width, missing the heteroscedasticity. The IQN, by jointly learning the dependence on both \(x\) and \(\tau\), captures both phenomena simultaneously without any explicit structural assumptions.


Show code (9 lines)


Code
# Run diagnostics on the Friedman example
cov_f = compute_coverage(model_fried, X_fried, y_fried, xm_f, xs_f, ym_f, ys_f)
print("Coverage analysis (Friedman 1D, training set):")
for level, emp in cov_f.items():
    print(f"  Nominal {level:.0%} -> Empirical {emp:.1%}")

nc_f, mv_f, fp_f = detect_crossings(model_fried,
    np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 100).reshape(-1, 1), xm_f, xs_f, ym_f, ys_f)
print(f"\nQuantile crossings: {nc_f} violations, max magnitude {mv_f:.4f}")




Show code (7 lines)

Coverage analysis (Friedman 1D, training set):
  Nominal 50% -> Empirical 50.0%
  Nominal 80% -> Empirical 74.5%
  Nominal 90% -> Empirical 87.0%
  Nominal 95% -> Empirical 93.5%

Quantile crossings: 7510 violations, max magnitude 0.8886

title: 5  Implicit Quantile Networks
text:
5.9 Exercises

Exercise 5.1 Cosine embedding from scratch. Implement the cosine embedding (Eq. 5.2) without using any deep learning library. Given \(\tau = 0.3\) and \(M = 8\), compute \(\varphi(\tau) \in \mathbb{R}^8\) by hand (or with NumPy). Plot the embedding vectors for \(\tau \in \{0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9\}\) as bar charts. What do you notice about how the embeddings change with \(\tau\)?


Exercise 5.2 Uniform sampling approximates CRPS/2. Show that if \(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_K\) are drawn i.i.d. from \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\), then \[
\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \rho_{\tau_k}(y - \hat{Q}(\tau_k \mid x)) \xrightarrow{K \to \infty} \frac{1}{2}\text{CRPS}(\hat{F}, y)
\] almost surely, where \(\hat{F}\) is the CDF implied by the quantile function \(\hat{Q}(\cdot \mid x)\). (The factor of 1/2 arises because CRPS = \(2\int_0^1 \rho_\tau \, d\tau\) per Eq. 5.5.) What is the convergence rate? Hint: Apply the strong law of large numbers and use the integral representation of CRPS (Eq. 5.5).


Exercise 5.3 Heteroscedastic sine function. Generate \(n = 500\) observations from the model \[
Y = \sin(x) + 0.1 \, |x| \, \varepsilon, \quad x \sim \text{Uniform}(-3, 3), \quad \varepsilon \sim N(0,1).
\] Train an IQN and plot the quantile fan (\(\tau \in \{0.05, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.95\}\)) overlaid on the data. Does the network correctly learn that the variance increases with \(|x|\)? Compare with a linear quantile regression fit.


Exercise 5.4 Cosine vs. linear embedding. Modify the IQN architecture to use a linear embedding: replace the cosine features with \(\phi_{\text{lin}}(\tau) = \text{ReLU}(w \cdot \tau + b)\) where \(\tau\) enters as a scalar. Train both versions on the motorcycle data for the same number of epochs and compare: (a) validation CRPS, (b) visual quality of the quantile fan, and (c) whether quantile crossings occur. What is the advantage of the cosine embedding?


Exercise 5.5 Build an IQN from scratch. Without using the IQN class from this chapter, implement a complete IQN from scratch using only torch.nn.Linear and activation functions. Your implementation should include the following steps: (a) implement the cosine embedding as a standalone function (not a class), (b) implement the covariate encoder as a two-layer MLP, (c) implement the multiplicative merge, (d) implement the output head, and (e) wire everything together in a forward method. Train your implementation on the synthetic data \(Y = x^2 + 0.3\varepsilon\), \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(-2, 2)\), \(\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)\), and verify that the predicted 50% quantile approximates the parabola \(x^2\).


Exercise 5.6 Additive vs. multiplicative architecture. Modify the IQN class to use an additive merge: replace h = h_x * h_tau with h = h_x + h_tau. Train both architectures on the motorcycle data for 2000 epochs with 5 different random seeds each. Compare: (a) the mean and standard deviation of the test CRPS, (b) the visual smoothness of the predicted quantile fans, and (c) the number of quantile crossings detected by detect_crossings. Which architecture is more stable across random seeds? Can you construct a synthetic dataset where the additive architecture performs as well as the multiplicative one?


Exercise 5.7 PIT histograms for model comparison. Generate \(n = 1000\) observations from the model \(Y = 2 + 3\sin(x) + (1 + |x|)\varepsilon\), \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(-\pi, \pi)\), \(\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)\). Fit three models: (a) an IQN with the default architecture, (b) an IQN with \(d = 16\) (deliberately too small), and (c) an IQN with 100 training epochs (deliberately too few). Produce PIT histograms for all three models on a held-out test set. Describe the specific shape of each PIT histogram and explain what it tells you about the model’s miscalibration. Which failures are worse in practice — underdispersion or bias?


Exercise 5.8 Hyperparameter tuning on a new problem. Consider the 2D function \(f(x_1, x_2) = \sin(x_1) \cdot \cos(x_2)\) with additive noise \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, 0.25)\), where \((x_1, x_2) \sim \text{Uniform}([0, 2\pi]^2)\). Generate \(n = 2000\) training points and \(n_{\text{test}} = 500\) test points. Conduct a grid search over hidden dimension \(d \in \{64, 128, 256\}\), cosine frequencies \(M \in \{16, 32, 64\}\), and epochs \(T \in \{1000, 2000, 3000\}\) (27 configurations total). For each configuration, train 3 models with different seeds and report the mean test CRPS. Present your results as a table and identify which hyperparameter has the largest effect. Does the answer change if you increase the noise to \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, 4)\)?


Exercise 5.9 CRPS convergence curves. Modify the train_iqn function to record the validation CRPS every 100 epochs. Train an IQN on the motorcycle data (80% train, 20% validation) for 5000 epochs and plot the validation CRPS as a function of epoch. At what epoch does the CRPS stabilize? Now repeat with the learning rate increased to \(\eta_0 = 0.01\) and decreased to \(\eta_0 = 10^{-4}\). How does the learning rate affect the convergence speed and final CRPS? Overlay all three curves on a single plot.


Exercise 5.10 Pinball vs. Huber quantile loss. Implement the Huber quantile loss (Eq. 5.7) with threshold \(\kappa\). Generate \(n = 500\) observations from a heavy-tailed model: \(Y = x + t_3 \cdot (1 + |x|/3)\) where \(t_3\) denotes a draw from the Student-\(t\) distribution with 3 degrees of freedom and \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(-3, 3)\). Train IQN models with: (a) standard pinball loss, (b) Huber quantile loss with \(\kappa = 0.5\), and (c) Huber quantile loss with \(\kappa = 2.0\). Compare the test CRPS and visual quality of the quantile fans in all three cases. Does the Huber variant help more or less than expected? What happens if you replace \(t_3\) with \(N(0,1)\) noise (light tails)?
