title: 14  When IQN Fails: Calibration and Remedies
text:
14.7 Diagnostic Checklist
We have now seen that IQN fails silently on high-SNR data and that even the het-MLP ensemble’s Gaussian intervals can be poorly calibrated. Unlike point prediction, where a single metric like RMSE reveals whether the model is working, uncertainty quantification can fail in subtle ways. A model can produce reasonable-looking prediction intervals that have entirely wrong coverage. It can produce correct marginal coverage while being wildly miscalibrated conditionally. It can appear well-calibrated on the training distribution but fail catastrophically under distribution shift. The IQN failure documented in Section 14.1 is a particularly insidious example: the model produces excellent point predictions (RMSE competitive with the GP baseline) while its uncertainty estimates are essentially meaningless (34% coverage at 90% nominal). Without a systematic diagnostic procedure, this failure would be invisible from point-prediction metrics alone.
The checklist follows four sequential diagnostic steps. If the first diagnostic reveals a problem, fix it before proceeding to the second. Each diagnostic has a specific indicator (what to look for), a diagnosis (what the problem is), and a remedy (what to do about it).






flowchart TD
    A["Train model and<br/>compute predictions"] --> B{"Check PIT histogram:<br/>uniform on [0,1]?"}
    B -- "Not uniform" --> B1["Model misspecification.<br/>Revise architecture or<br/>input features."]
    B -- "Approximately uniform" --> C{"Check CRPS vs. epoch:<br/>still decreasing?"}
    C -- "Plateaus high" --> C1["Underfitting.<br/>Increase capacity,<br/>train longer,<br/>or reduce regularization."]
    C -- "Converged" --> D{"Check quantile crossings:<br/>frequent?"}
    D -- "Frequent crossings" --> D1["Architecture problem.<br/>Use monotone output layer<br/>or switch to het-MLP."]
    D -- "Rare or none" --> E{"Check coverage:<br/>within 5% of nominal?"}
    E -- "Off by > 5%" --> E1["Calibration failure.<br/>Apply conformal<br/>post-processing."]
    E -- "Within 5%" --> F["Model is well-calibrated.<br/>Deploy."]




Figure 14.4: Diagnostic flowchart for IQN and neural network uncertainty quantification. Each node represents a diagnostic check; edges lead to either the next check (if passed) or a remedy (if failed).





The flowchart should be read top-to-bottom: each check either passes (leading to the next check) or fails (leading to a specific remedy). We now describe each diagnostic in detail, including practical guidance on how to implement each check.
Step 1: PIT histogram. The probability integral transform (PIT) maps each observation \(y_i\) through the model’s predicted CDF: \(u_i = \hat{F}(y_i \mid x_i)\). If the model is correctly specified, the PIT values \(u_1, \ldots, u_n\) should be approximately \(\text{Uniform}(0, 1)\). For a het-MLP, the PIT is computed as \(u_i = \Phi((y_i - \hat{\mu}(x_i)) / \hat{\sigma}(x_i))\) where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. For an IQN, it is computed by inverting the learned quantile function: \(u_i = \hat{F}(y_i \mid x_i)\) where \(\hat{F}\) is the CDF implied by the quantile predictions. In practice, we find \(\tau^*\) by binary search over \(\tau \in (0,1)\) such that \(\hat{Q}(\tau^* \mid x_i) = y_i\), then set \(u_i = \tau^*\). The package provides a utility for this numerical inversion. A U-shaped PIT histogram indicates underdispersion (prediction intervals too narrow). An inverted-U shape indicates overdispersion (intervals too wide). A skewed histogram indicates bias in the location. If the PIT histogram is far from uniform, the model is fundamentally misspecified — neither adding capacity nor applying conformal calibration will fix the underlying problem. Revisit the architecture, the input features, or the loss function.
Step 2: CRPS vs. epoch. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) is the integral of the pinball loss across all quantile levels, as we defined in Section 5.5.2. Monitoring CRPS on a validation set during training reveals whether the model has converged. If the CRPS plateaus at a high value early in training, the model is underfitting: it lacks the capacity or the training time to learn the conditional distribution. Increase the network width or depth, train for more epochs, or reduce regularization. If the CRPS is still decreasing at the end of training, the model needs more epochs. For het-MLP models, the analogous diagnostic is to monitor the Gaussian NLL on a held-out validation set: if it is still decreasing, the model has not converged. A useful secondary check is to plot the validation NLL alongside the training NLL: if the training NLL continues to decrease while the validation NLL increases, the model is overfitting and needs regularization (dropout, weight decay, or early stopping).
Step 3: Quantile crossings. For any \(\tau_1 < \tau_2\), the true quantile function satisfies \(Q(\tau_1 \mid x) \leq Q(\tau_2 \mid x)\) for all \(x\). The IQN does not enforce this monotonicity constraint, and quantile crossings — where the 0.05 quantile exceeds the 0.95 quantile, for example — indicate that the architecture is struggling to produce a coherent distributional prediction. Occasional crossings (less than 1% of test points) are harmless and can be fixed by post-hoc sorting of the predicted quantiles. Frequent crossings (more than 5%) signal a fundamental architectural problem: the multiplicative \(\tau\)-embedding cannot express the required distributional structure at this SNR level. On the lake data, the standard IQN produces crossings at 12% of test points, confirming the severity of the failure. The remedy is either a monotone output layer that enforces non-crossing by construction (such as the increasing-softmax architecture of Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val, and Galichon (2010)), or a switch to the het-MLP approach where the Gaussian distributional assumption prevents crossings entirely, since \(\hat{\mu}(x) - z \hat{\sigma}(x) < \hat{\mu}(x) + z \hat{\sigma}(x)\) for any \(z > 0\) and \(\hat{\sigma}(x) > 0\).
Step 4: Coverage. Finally, check the empirical coverage of the prediction intervals at the nominal level. If coverage is within 5 percentage points of the target (e.g., 85–95% at a 90% nominal level), the model is reasonably well-calibrated and can be deployed, possibly with minor conformal adjustments. If coverage is off by more than 5 percentage points — as in our IQN experiments where coverage was 11–34% at a 90% target — conformal post-processing is essential. When checking coverage, it is important to check it at multiple nominal levels (e.g., 50%, 80%, 90%, 95%) and across subgroups of the data (e.g., different horizons, different seasons, different depth layers). A model that achieves 90% overall coverage but only 60% coverage at long horizons is miscalibrated in a practically important way that overall metrics miss.
The flowchart in Figure 14.4 is designed to be followed sequentially. A model that fails Step 1 should not be conformally calibrated (Step 4) — conformal calibration can correct the scale of prediction intervals but not their shape, so a fundamentally misspecified model will produce conformal intervals that are correctly sized on average but poorly adapted to the local structure. Fix the model first, then calibrate.
The checklist is intentionally sequential because each diagnostic is most informative when the earlier checks have passed. A model with severe misspecification (Step 1) will have poor CRPS (Step 2), frequent quantile crossings (Step 3), and bad coverage (Step 4) — but fixing the misspecification may resolve all four problems simultaneously. Diagnosing the root cause saves time.
To make the checklist concrete, consider how it applies to our two main examples. On the motorcycle data from Section 5.7, the IQN passes all four steps: the PIT histogram is approximately uniform (the distributional model captures the heteroscedastic, non-Gaussian structure), CRPS converges to a low value, quantile crossings are rare (less than 0.5% of test points), and coverage is within 2 percentage points of nominal. The IQN is the right tool for that problem. On the lake temperature data, the IQN fails at Step 4: coverage is 34% at a 90% target, and the PI width does not vary meaningfully across nominal levels. The checklist directs us to conformal post-processing, and since the underlying model is fundamentally unable to produce spread (an architecture problem, not just a calibration problem), it further suggests switching to the het-MLP. Following the checklist systematically would have saved us the time spent trying larger IQNs and two-stage approaches — all of which failed for the same architectural reason.

text:
14.8 When to Use Conformal Post-Processing
The conformal calibration pipeline developed in Section 14.4 is not always necessary. When should a practitioner invest in conformal post-processing, and when is the model’s native uncertainty sufficient?
Conformal prediction provides a marginal coverage guarantee: the probability that the prediction interval contains a randomly drawn test point is at least \(1 - \alpha\). This guarantee is averaged over both the randomness in the calibration data and the randomness in the test point. It does not guarantee conditional coverage — that is, it does not promise that coverage is \(1 - \alpha\) for every value of \(x\). As Section 11.2 discussed, this distinction matters: marginal coverage is weaker but always achievable, while conditional coverage is stronger but generally impossible without distributional assumptions. Vovk (2012) showed that exact conditional coverage is impossible in a distribution-free setting: for any calibration procedure, there exists a distribution under which the conditional coverage at some \(x\) is arbitrarily far from the nominal level.
We recommend conformal post-processing in three situations.
First, when the model’s native coverage is off by more than 5 percentage points from the target. If a het-MLP ensemble achieves 84% coverage at a 90% nominal level, the miscalibration is modest and may be acceptable for exploratory analysis. But if IQN achieves 34% coverage at a 90% target, conformal calibration is essential — the native intervals are meaningless. The lake temperature benchmark is an extreme case of this scenario: the IQN coverage of 11–34% is so far from the target that conformal calibration on IQN outputs would produce extremely wide intervals. The better approach, as we demonstrated, is to switch to a het-MLP first and then apply conformal calibration to get the scale right. The 5-percentage-point threshold is a pragmatic guideline, not a hard rule: the decision should also consider the downstream consequences of miscalibration and the cost of implementing conformal calibration (which requires a separate calibration phase and slightly more complex deployment infrastructure).
Second, when the deployment context requires guaranteed coverage. In operational forecasting — such as the lake temperature forecasts used for water treatment decisions — the consequences of systematically overconfident intervals can be severe. A water treatment plant that relies on an 85% coverage interval for algal bloom prediction needs that 85% to be real, not an aspirational lower bound. Conformal calibration converts model-dependent coverage claims into distribution-free guarantees (up to the exchangeability assumption), which is a substantial improvement in reliability. The coverage guarantee is marginal — it holds on average over the randomness in both the calibration data and the test point — but marginal coverage with a rigorous guarantee is often more useful in practice than conditional coverage with no guarantee at all.
Third, when the data is non-stationary. In time-series applications, the test distribution systematically differs from the training distribution: new seasons bring new weather patterns, lake conditions evolve, and the physics-based simulator may be updated. The temporal CV approach in Section 14.4.1 generates calibration residuals that span multiple seasons and years, providing some robustness to distributional shift. Without conformal calibration, the model’s native variance estimates are trained on historical data and may be poorly calibrated for future conditions. This is perhaps the strongest argument for conformal post-processing in time-series settings: it provides a principled way to account for the fact that the future is different from the past, without requiring an explicit model of how the distribution shifts.
Conversely, conformal post-processing may be unnecessary or even counterproductive in two situations. When the model is already well-calibrated (coverage within 2–3 percentage points of the target), conformal calibration adds little value and may slightly widen the intervals. And when conditional coverage is paramount, the constant-width conformal intervals may be less useful than adaptive intervals from a well-calibrated model. In such cases, the conformalized quantile regression approach of Romano, Patterson, and Candès (2019) — which we discussed in Section 11.2.1 — provides adaptive intervals with marginal coverage guarantees by using \(\max(\hat{Q}(\alpha/2 \mid x) - y, y - \hat{Q}(1-\alpha/2 \mid x))\) as the nonconformity score, combining the best of both worlds, provided the base model’s quantile estimates are reasonable.
A rule of thumb from our experience across the benchmarks in this book. On the motorcycle and Phantom datasets, the IQN produces well-calibrated intervals without any conformal correction — the distributional flexibility of the quantile regression approach is both necessary and sufficient. On the lake temperature data, conformal calibration is essential because the base model’s uncertainty estimates are unreliable. The dividing line is, roughly, whether the base model’s coverage is within 5 percentage points of the target. Below that threshold, conformal calibration is the right investment. Above it, the effort is better spent on improving the base model itself.
Conformal calibration should be re-run periodically in non-stationary settings. The conformal quantiles are computed from a specific set of out-of-fold residuals, which reflect the error structure at a particular point in time. As the data-generating process evolves — due to climate change, changes in reservoir management, or updates to the physics-based simulator — the old conformal quantiles may become stale. A practical approach is to update the conformal quantiles (Phase 1 only, without retraining the ensemble) whenever new data accumulates, using an expanding window of recent forecast–observation pairs. This provides a lightweight way to maintain calibration over time without the full cost of retraining. In our lake temperature application, this could be implemented by collecting forecast–observation pairs during each season and updating the per-horizon conformal quantiles at the start of each new season, using all accumulated data. The neural network ensemble would be retrained only when the accumulated performance degradation (measured by RMSE or coverage) exceeds a predetermined threshold.

title: 14  When IQN Fails: Calibration and Remedies
text:
14.9 Summary: When to Use What
This chapter has presented a diagnostic and a remedy for IQN failure on high-SNR data. The broader message is that the choice of uncertainty quantification method should match the problem characteristics.



Table 14.5: Recommended uncertainty quantification approach by problem type.










Problem type
Recommended approach
Why




Heteroscedastic, multimodal
IQN (Chapter 5)
Full distributional flexibility; no parametric assumption


Jump discontinuities
Aug-IQN (Chapter 8)
Boundary augmentation handles piecewise structure


High SNR, Gaussian-like noise
Het-MLP ensemble + conformal
IQN gradient collapse; parametric variance + conformal


Small \(n\), low \(d\)
GP (Chapters 7.1)
GP prior beneficial; principled posterior uncertainty






The diagnostic is the signal-to-noise ratio. When fitting a good point predictor leaves residuals that are a small fraction of the response range, the IQN architecture will struggle to produce distributional spread. In that regime, the het-MLP ensemble with conformal calibration is the right tool.
The diagnostic checklist in Section 14.7 provides a systematic procedure for evaluating any neural network UQ method on a new dataset. Follow it sequentially: check the PIT histogram for distributional misspecification, monitor CRPS convergence for underfitting, inspect quantile crossings for architectural problems, and validate coverage for calibration failure. If the model passes all four checks, deploy it with confidence. If it fails at any step, the checklist points to the appropriate remedy. The entire diagnostic procedure can be run in minutes, even on large datasets, and should be standard practice before deploying any neural network uncertainty model.
This chapter completes a natural arc. We began in Chapter 5 with the IQN as a universal tool for conditional distributions, demonstrated its power on heteroscedastic (Section 5.7) and multimodal (Chapter 8) problems, and used it to build surrogates (Chapter 7) and drive active learning (Chapter 9). Here we have shown its limits and provided an alternative. The GBC framework is broader than any single architecture: it encompasses IQN when distributional flexibility is needed, het-MLP ensembles when parametric models suffice, and conformal calibration when distribution-free guarantees are required.
Uncertainty quantification is harder than point prediction, and no single method works everywhere. Conformal calibration provides a safety net for either approach, converting model-dependent uncertainty estimates into distribution-free prediction intervals with honest coverage.
In the language of the GBC framework, this chapter demonstrates that “generative Bayesian computation” is not synonymous with “implicit quantile networks.” The GBC philosophy — simulate from the model, train a neural network, produce posterior quantiles — encompasses multiple architectures and calibration strategies. The het-MLP ensemble with conformal calibration is a GBC method: it produces calibrated predictive distributions without evaluating a likelihood, without running MCMC chains, and without specifying a prior. It just happens to use Gaussian NLL rather than pinball loss, and conformal quantiles rather than IQN quantiles. The computational philosophy is the same; only the implementation differs.

text:
14.10 Exercises
The exercises below progress from theoretical properties of the failure mode (Exercises 14.1–14.2) through hands-on implementation of the calibration pipeline (Exercises 14.3–14.4) to diagnostic and design questions that require experimental investigation (Exercises 14.5–14.8). We recommend completing at least Exercises 14.1, 14.3, and 14.6, which cover the core concepts of the chapter: the SNR diagnostic, conformal calibration, and gradient collapse. Exercise 14.4 is the most comprehensive and provides a complete end-to-end implementation of the GBC calibration pipeline on the lake temperature data.

Exercise 14.1 Signal-to-noise diagnostic.
Consider a regression problem where \(Y \mid X = x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu(x), \sigma^2)\) with a known constant variance \(\sigma^2\).

Define the signal-to-noise ratio as \(\text{SNR} = \text{Var}(\mu(X)) / \sigma^2\), where \(\text{Var}(\mu(X))\) is the variance of the conditional mean across the input distribution. Show that the width of the 90% prediction interval \(F^{-1}_{Y|X}(0.95) - F^{-1}_{Y|X}(0.05)\) equals \(2 \times 1.645 \sigma\) and does not depend on \(\text{SNR}\).
Now consider the IQN’s quantile prediction \(\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x) = g_\theta(\psi_\theta(x) \odot \phi_\theta(\tau))\). Suppose the covariate encoder \(\psi_\theta(x)\) has learned \(\mu(x)\) perfectly. Write down the condition on \(\phi_\theta(\tau)\) that would produce the correct 90% PI width. Why is this condition hard for the IQN to learn when \(\text{SNR} \gg 1\)?
Generate synthetic data with \(n = 5000\), \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(-3, 3)\), \(\mu(x) = 5 \sin(x)\), and \(\sigma = 0.1\). Train an IQN (128$$2, cosine \(\tau\)-embedding, 2000 epochs) and a het-MLP (128$$2, 2000 epochs) on this data. Compare their 90% PI coverage on a held-out test set. Repeat with \(\sigma = 1.0\) and \(\sigma = 5.0\). At what \(\text{SNR}\) does the IQN begin to fail? Plot coverage vs. \(\sigma\) for both methods.
For the \(\sigma = 0.1\) case, plot the IQN’s learned quantiles \(\hat{Q}(0.05 \mid x)\), \(\hat{Q}(0.50 \mid x)\), and \(\hat{Q}(0.95 \mid x)\) as functions of \(x\), overlaid on the data. Compare with the het-MLP’s intervals \(\hat{\mu}(x) \pm 1.645 \hat{\sigma}(x)\). How do the two methods differ visually?



Exercise 14.2 Gaussian NLL properties.

Show that the Gaussian NLL loss (Eq. 14.11) has a unique minimum at \(\hat{\mu}(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]\) and \(\hat{\sigma}^2(x) = \text{Var}(Y \mid X = x)\) in the population limit (i.e., minimizing \(\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}]\)).
Compare the gradients of the Gaussian NLL with respect to \(\mu\) and \(\log \sigma^2\). Show that the gradient with respect to \(\log \sigma^2\) is \(\frac{1}{2}(1 - (y - \mu)^2 / \sigma^2)\). Interpret this: when is the gradient positive (pushing \(\sigma^2\) down) vs. negative (pushing \(\sigma^2\) up)?
A common failure mode of Gaussian NLL training is variance collapse: the network drives \(\hat{\sigma}^2(x) \to 0\) at a subset of training points, causing the loss to diverge. Explain why the \(\log \sigma^2\) parameterization mitigates but does not eliminate this issue. Propose a practical remedy (hint: clamp the variance from below).



Exercise 14.3 Conformal calibration.
Generate \(n = 5000\) observations from \(Y = \sin(2\pi x) + \epsilon\) where \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) and \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1^2)\).

Train a het-MLP ensemble (\(K = 3\), 256$$2, 2000 epochs) on the first 4000 observations. Compute Gaussian prediction intervals \(\bar{\mu}(x) \pm z_{0.95} \cdot \sigma_{\text{ens}}(x)\) on the last 1000 observations. Report the 90% coverage. Is the ensemble well-calibrated?
Implement split conformal calibration: use 500 of the 4000 training observations as a calibration set. Compute the 90th percentile of \(|y_i - \bar{\mu}(x_i)|\) on the calibration set. Apply this to form conformal PIs on the test set. Report coverage and compare with (a).
Now repeat with heteroscedastic noise: \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, (0.05 + 0.2x)^2)\). Compare the conformal intervals (constant width) with the Gaussian intervals (varying width). Which method achieves better conditional coverage? Which has better average PI width?



Exercise 14.4 Lake temperature analysis.
This exercise uses the lake temperature data from Section 14.6. Download the dataset from the book’s repository.

Train a single het-MLP (256$$3, 5000 epochs) on the training data. Compute the Gaussian PI coverage (90% target) overall and at horizons \(h = 1, 10, 30\). Confirm that the Gaussian coverage is around 49%.
Add an IQN (same architecture as the het-MLP backbone: 256$$3, 3000 epochs) and compute its 90% PI coverage. Confirm that coverage is 30–40%. Inspect the PI width: is it much narrower than the het-MLP’s Gaussian intervals?
Implement the 5-fold temporal CV conformal calibration pipeline. Compare pooled conformal quantiles (single \(\hat{q}_{0.90}\)) vs. per-horizon quantiles (\(\hat{q}_{0.90}(h)\)). Report the overall coverage and the per-horizon coverage at \(h = 1, 15, 30\) for both approaches. Which is closer to the 90% target at each horizon?
Vary the ensemble size \(K \in \{1, 3, 5, 10\}\) and report the overall RMSE. At what \(K\) does the marginal improvement become negligible? Plot RMSE vs. \(K\).



Exercise 14.5 PIT diagnostics.
The probability integral transform (PIT) is a key diagnostic for distributional models, as discussed in the diagnostic checklist (Section 14.7). In this exercise, we explore how different types of miscalibration manifest in the PIT histogram, building intuition for interpreting PIT plots in practice.

Generate \(n = 2000\) observations from \(Y = x^2 + \epsilon\) where \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(-2, 2)\) and \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2)\). Train a het-MLP (128$$2, 1000 epochs) and compute PIT values \(u_i = \Phi((y_i - \hat{\mu}(x_i)) / \hat{\sigma}(x_i))\) where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. Plot the PIT histogram. Is the model well-calibrated?
Now generate data with \(t\)-distributed noise: \(\epsilon \sim t_3 \cdot 0.3 / \sqrt{3}\) (scaled to have the same variance as the Gaussian case). Train the same het-MLP and compute PIT values. The PIT histogram should show a U-shaped pattern. Explain why: what does a U-shape indicate about the model’s prediction intervals relative to the true distribution?
Fit a conformal calibration layer on top of the het-MLP from (b). Does conformal calibration fix the U-shape in the PIT histogram, or does it only fix the marginal coverage? Discuss the distinction between marginal and conditional calibration in light of your results.



Exercise 14.6 Gradient collapse experiment.
This exercise provides hands-on experience with the gradient collapse mechanism described in Section 14.1.1. By varying the noise level \(\sigma\) in a controlled synthetic experiment, we can observe the transition from well-calibrated IQN behavior to the gradient collapse regime.

Generate \(n = 5000\) observations from \(Y = 10 \sin(x) + \sigma \epsilon\) where \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(-\pi, \pi)\) and \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). Train an IQN (128$$2, 2000 epochs, cosine \(\tau\)-embedding with 64 dimensions) for each \(\sigma \in \{0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0\}\). For each \(\sigma\), compute the average PI width \(\overline{W} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i [\hat{Q}(0.95 \mid x_i) - \hat{Q}(0.05 \mid x_i)]\) and the 90% PI coverage. Plot both quantities against \(\sigma\). At what noise level does the PI width begin to collapse?
For the \(\sigma = 0.1\) case, monitor the gradient norm \(\|\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \theta_\tau\|\) (the gradient with respect to the quantile-encoder parameters only) during training. You can compute this by calling loss.backward() and then summing the squared gradients of all parameters in the quantile-embedding layers. Compare this to \(\|\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \theta_x\|\) (the gradient with respect to the covariate-encoder parameters). How does the ratio \(\|\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \theta_\tau\| / \|\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \theta_x\|\) evolve over epochs? Does the quantile-encoder gradient vanish as the mean fit improves? Plot the ratio on a log scale.
Repeat (a) using a het-MLP ensemble (\(K = 3\)) with conformal calibration. Show that the het-MLP + conformal approach maintains valid coverage across all \(\sigma\) values, unlike the IQN.



Exercise 14.7 Temporal vs. random cross-validation.
This exercise demonstrates why temporal CV is essential for time-series calibration. The distinction between temporal and random CV is subtle but consequential: random CV produces overly optimistic residuals because the model trains on data from both before and after the held-out fold, effectively “seeing the future.”

Generate a non-stationary time series: \(y_t = \sin(2\pi t / 365) + 0.005 t + \epsilon_t\) for \(t = 1, \ldots, 1000\), where \(\epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5^2)\). The term \(0.005 t\) introduces a linear trend. Use the first 800 observations for training and the last 200 for testing.
Perform 5-fold random CV on the training data: randomly assign observations to folds, train a het-MLP on 4 folds, predict on the held-out fold, and collect residuals. Compute the conformal quantile \(\hat{q}_{0.90}\) from the pooled residuals. Apply it to the test set and report coverage.
Perform 5-fold temporal CV on the training data: assign observations to 5 consecutive blocks of 160 observations each. Repeat the same procedure. Report coverage on the test set.
Compare the coverage from (b) and (c). Which is closer to 90%? Explain why random CV produces overly optimistic residuals when the data has a temporal trend. Specifically, in random CV, the training set for each fold includes observations from after the held-out fold — the model “sees the future” and produces smaller residuals than it would in a genuine forecast setting. What happens if you increase the trend coefficient from 0.005 to 0.02?
As a further experiment, compare the conformal quantile \(\hat{q}_{0.90}\) from random CV vs. temporal CV. Which is smaller? By how much? How does this translate to PI width and coverage on the test set?



Exercise 14.8 Ensemble size and uncertainty decomposition.
This exercise explores how ensemble size \(K\) affects the decomposition of uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, as described in Eq. 14.9. Understanding this decomposition is essential for interpreting ensemble predictions and for deciding how many ensemble members to train.

Generate \(n = 3000\) observations from \(Y = \sin(3x) + (0.1 + 0.3 |x|) \epsilon\) where \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(-3, 3)\) and \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). Train het-MLP ensembles with \(K \in \{1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20\}\) members (128$$2, 2000 epochs each). For each \(K\), compute the average aleatoric uncertainty \(\bar{\sigma}^2_{\text{aleatoric}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \frac{1}{K} \sum_k \hat{\sigma}^2_k(x_i)\) and the average epistemic uncertainty \(\bar{\sigma}^2_{\text{epistemic}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i [\frac{1}{K} \sum_k \hat{\mu}^2_k(x_i) - \bar{\mu}^2(x_i)]\). Plot both as a function of \(K\).
As \(K\) grows, the epistemic component should decrease (members agree more on average) while the aleatoric component should stabilize (it reflects irreducible noise, not model uncertainty). At what \(K\) does the epistemic component become less than 10% of the aleatoric component?
Evaluate the 90% PI coverage on a held-out test set (\(n = 1000\)) for each \(K\), using both Gaussian intervals and conformal intervals (with a calibration set of 500 observations). Does coverage improve monotonically with \(K\)? Is there a diminishing returns effect? Which approach — Gaussian or conformal — benefits more from increasing the ensemble size?
Discuss the computational tradeoff. Each additional ensemble member roughly doubles the training time but provides diminishing improvement in RMSE and coverage. If training time is the binding constraint, is it better to train \(K = 3\) members for 4000 epochs each, or \(K = 10\) members for 1200 epochs each (same total compute)? Implement both configurations and compare.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
text:
A.1 Universal Approximation
This appendix collects the main approximation-theoretic and convergence results that underpin the GBC framework. The proofs are organized to follow the logical chain: universal approximation guarantees that neural networks can represent quantile functions (Section A.1), the CRPS bound connects pointwise quantile accuracy to distributional accuracy (Section A.2), consistency establishes that the empirical risk minimizer converges to the true quantile function (Section A.3), the CRPS convergence theorem shows that the distributional accuracy of the IQN improves as capacity and data grow (Section A.4), minimax rates quantify the optimal speed of convergence and compositional depth breaks the curse of dimensionality (Section A.5–A.6), and the autoregressive noise outsourcing theorem extends the entire program to multivariate parameters (Section A.7).
Throughout, we use the following notation. The input domain is \(\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), assumed compact unless otherwise stated. The conditional quantile function is \(Q^*(\tau, x) = F_{Y|X}^{-1}(\tau \mid x)\) for \(\tau \in (0,1)\) and \(x \in \mathcal{X}\). The pinball (check) loss is \(\rho_\tau(u) = u(\tau - \mathbf{1}(u < 0))\). The CRPS of a predictive quantile function \(G\) at observation \(y\) is \(\mathrm{CRPS}(G, y) = 2\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(y - G(\tau, x))\,d\tau\). A ReLU network class \(\mathcal{G}(L, W)\) consists of feedforward networks with depth \(L\), maximum width \(W\), and ReLU activations \(\sigma(z) = \max(0, z)\).
The universal approximation theorem guarantees that feedforward neural networks can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain to arbitrary accuracy. This result, due to Hornik, Stinchcombe, and White (1989), provides the existence guarantee for GBC: the conditional quantile function \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) can be represented by a neural network.
Proof. The proof proceeds via the Hahn-Banach theorem. Define the set \(\mathcal{H} = \{z \mapsto \sigma(w^\top z + b) : w \in \mathbb{R}^p, b \in \mathbb{R}\}\). Suppose, for contradiction, that the closed linear span of \(\mathcal{H}\) is not all of \(C(K)\). By the Hahn-Banach theorem, there exists a nonzero bounded linear functional \(L\) on \(C(K)\) that annihilates every element of \(\mathcal{H}\). By the Riesz representation theorem, \(L\) corresponds to a nonzero signed measure \(\mu\) on \(K\) such that \(\int \sigma(w^\top x + b)\,d\mu(x) = 0\) for all \((w, b) \in \mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}\). The Fourier analysis argument of Leshno et al. (1993) then shows that this integral condition forces \(\mu = 0\), a contradiction. Concretely, Leshno et al. (1993) show that if \(\sigma\) is locally bounded and not a polynomial (which holds for any non-constant bounded monotone-increasing function), then the only measure annihilating all half-space sigmoids is the zero measure. Hence \(\mathrm{span}(\mathcal{H})\) is dense in \(C(K)\), which is precisely the claim. See Leshno et al. (1993) for the complete proof. \(\square\)
The original theorem uses sigmoidal activations. The extension to ReLU activations follows from Leshno et al. (1993), who proved that a single-hidden-layer network is a universal approximator if and only if the activation function is non-polynomial. Since ReLU is non-polynomial, universal approximation holds. Schmidt-Hieber (2020) provides the ReLU-specific result with explicit rate bounds for deep networks.
The logarithmic depth is significant: deep networks achieve the same approximation accuracy as wide shallow networks but with exponentially fewer parameters when the target function has compositional structure. This is the approximation-theoretic basis for the advantage of depth.
The IQN architecture processes \((\tau, x)\) via a cosine embedding \(\varphi(\tau) = (\cos(\pi j \tau))_{j=0}^{M-1}\) and an elementwise product \(f_x(x) \odot f_\tau(\varphi(\tau))\), followed by fully connected layers. To apply Theorem A.1, we must verify that this architecture retains universal approximation.
Proof. The cosine embedding \(\varphi : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^M\) is a fixed continuous injection (for \(M \geq 2\)). Let \(r = p + q\) be the hidden dimension. Define \(f_x(x) = [h_x(x); \mathbf{1}_q] \in \mathbb{R}^r\) and \(f_\tau(\varphi(\tau)) = [\mathbf{1}_p; h_\tau(\tau)] \in \mathbb{R}^r\), where the constant blocks are realized via bias terms. Then \[
f_x(x) \odot f_\tau(\varphi(\tau)) = [h_x(x); \, h_\tau(\tau)],
\] which is a concatenation of features from both branches. The subsequent fully connected layers applied to this concatenation form a standard feedforward network on the joint representation \((h_x(x), h_\tau(\tau))\). By Theorem A.1, this is a universal approximator on the compact domain \([0,1] \times \mathcal{X}\) for sufficiently large \(p\), \(q\), and hidden widths. \(\square\)

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
text:
TipTheorem A.1: Universal Approximation (Hornik, Stinchcombe, and White 1989)



Let \(K \subset \mathbb{R}^p\) be compact and let \(f : K \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous. For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a single-hidden-layer network \[
h(z) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \alpha_j \, \sigma(w_j^\top z + b_j) + c
\] with \(m\) hidden units, where \(\sigma\) is any non-constant, bounded, monotone-increasing activation function, such that \(\sup_{z \in K} |h(z) - f(z)| < \varepsilon\).










TipTheorem A.2: Universal Approximation for Deep ReLU Networks



Let \(K \subset \mathbb{R}^p\) be compact and let \(f : K \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous. For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a ReLU network \(h_\phi : K \to \mathbb{R}\) with depth \(L\) and total parameters \(N\) such that \(\sup_{z \in K} |h_\phi(z) - f(z)| < \varepsilon\).
Moreover, if \(f\) is \(\beta\)-Holder smooth (i.e., \(f \in C^\beta(K)\) with \(\beta > 0\)), then the approximation can be achieved with \(L = O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) layers and \(N = O(\varepsilon^{-p/\beta} \log(1/\varepsilon))\) parameters (Schmidt-Hieber 2020). The \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) factor arises from the depth required to implement multiplication via ReLU composition; it appears in both the layer count and the parameter count.










TipProposition A.1: Universal Approximation of the IQN Architecture



Let \(\mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) be compact and let \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) be a continuous conditional quantile function on \([0,1] \times \mathcal{X}\). For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an IQN with cosine embedding dimension \(M\) and hidden dimension \(r\) such that \(\sup_{\tau \in [0,1],\, x \in \mathcal{X}} |G_\phi(\tau, x) - Q^*(\tau, x)| < \varepsilon\).

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
text:
A.2 CRPS Approximation Bound
The CRPS measures the quality of a full predictive distribution. The following result shows that pointwise accuracy of quantile estimates translates directly into CRPS accuracy, with a tight multiplicative constant.






TipTheorem A.3: CRPS Approximation Bound



Let \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) denote the true conditional quantile function and \(G_\phi(\tau, x)\) an approximation satisfying \(\sup_{\tau \in [0,1]} |G_\phi(\tau, x) - Q^*(\tau, x)| \leq \varepsilon\) for a given \(x\). Then for any observation \(y\), \[
|\mathrm{CRPS}(G_\phi, y) - \mathrm{CRPS}(Q^*, y)| \leq 2\varepsilon.
\]


Proof. By Gneiting and Raftery (2007), the CRPS admits the quantile representation \[
\mathrm{CRPS}(F, y) = 2\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(y - F^{-1}(\tau))\,d\tau.
\] The pinball loss satisfies the Lipschitz bound \(|\rho_\tau(y - q_1) - \rho_\tau(y - q_2)| \leq |q_1 - q_2|\) for all \(q_1, q_2 \in \mathbb{R}\). To verify this, note that \(\rho_\tau(y - q)\) is piecewise linear in \(q\) with slopes \(-\tau\) (when \(q < y\)) and \(1 - \tau\) (when \(q > y\)). Both slopes are bounded in absolute value by \(\max(\tau, 1-\tau) \leq 1\), so \(\rho_\tau\) is 1-Lipschitz in \(q\).
Applying this bound under the integral: \[
\begin{aligned}
|\mathrm{CRPS}(G_\phi, y) - \mathrm{CRPS}(Q^*, y)| &= 2\left|\int_0^1 \left[\rho_\tau(y - G_\phi(\tau,x)) - \rho_\tau(y - Q^*(\tau, x))\right] d\tau\right| \\
&\leq 2\int_0^1 |G_\phi(\tau,x) - Q^*(\tau, x)|\,d\tau \leq 2\varepsilon. \quad \square
\end{aligned}
\]






NoteRemark A.1: Tightness



The constant \(2\) is tight. If \(G_\phi(\tau, x) = Q^*(\tau, x) + \varepsilon\) for all \(\tau\) (a uniform upward shift), then \(\mathrm{CRPS}(G_\phi, y) - \mathrm{CRPS}(Q^*, y) = 2\varepsilon\) for \(y\) below the support of \(Q^*\). The bound cannot be improved without additional assumptions.


The CRPS bound can also be expressed in terms of the Wasserstein distance. Recall from Chapter 4 that the 1-Wasserstein distance between distributions \(F\) and \(G\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is \[
W_1(F, G) = \int_0^1 |F^{-1}(\tau) - G^{-1}(\tau)|\,d\tau.
\]






TipCorollary A.1: CRPS and Wasserstein Distance



The expected CRPS satisfies \[
\mathbb{E}_Y[\mathrm{CRPS}(G_\phi, Y)] = 2\int_0^1 \mathbb{E}_Y[\rho_\tau(Y - G_\phi(\tau, X))]\,d\tau,
\] and when \(G_\phi\) is the quantile function of a distribution \(\hat{F}\), the CRPS admits the kernel representation from Gneiting and Raftery (2007): \[
\mathrm{CRPS}(\hat{F}, y) = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{F}}|X - y| - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\hat{F}}|X - X'|,
\] where \(X, X' \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \hat{F}\). The first term measures calibration (distance to the observation) and the second is a sharpness penalty (spread of the predictive distribution). Taking expectations over \(Y \sim F_{Y|X}\) and rearranging gives \(\mathbb{E}_Y[\mathrm{CRPS}(\hat{F}, Y)] = \mathbb{E}_Y \mathbb{E}_{\hat{F}}|X - Y| - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\hat{F}}|X - X'|\). When \(\hat{F} = F_{Y|X}\), the first term reduces to \(\mathbb{E}|Y - Y'|\) and the CRPS equals \(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|Y - Y'|\), the irreducible minimum.


This connects the training objective (integrated pinball loss over random \(\tau\)) directly to the Wasserstein metric on distributions. Minimizing the pinball loss is equivalent to minimizing the Wasserstein-1 distance between the learned and true conditional distributions.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
section: A.3 Consistency of the IQN Estimator
text:
A.3 Consistency of the IQN Estimator
The consistency theorem establishes that the empirical pinball-loss minimizer over a growing class of neural networks converges to the true conditional quantile function as the sample size increases.






TipTheorem A.4: Consistency of the Neural Quantile Estimator



Assume:

\(\mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) is compact and \(Y\) is bounded almost surely.
The conditional quantile function \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) is \(\beta\)-Holder continuous on \([0,1] \times \mathcal{X}\) for some \(\beta > 0\).
The network class \(\mathcal{G}_n = \mathcal{G}(L_n, W_n)\) consists of ReLU networks whose depth \(L_n\) and width \(W_n\) satisfy \(L_n W_n \log(L_n W_n) = o(n / \log n)\).

Then the empirical quantile loss minimizer \[
\hat{G}_n = \arg\min_{G \in \mathcal{G}_n} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \int_0^1 \rho_\tau(Y_i - G(\tau, X_i))\,d\tau
\] satisfies \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(Y - \hat{G}_n(\tau, X))\,d\tau\right] \longrightarrow \inf_G \mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(Y - G(\tau, X))\,d\tau\right]
\] as \(n \to \infty\). (Convergence is in expectation over the training set distribution, via the Rademacher complexity bound; almost sure or in-probability statements require additional arguments.)


Proof. The proof uses the standard bias–variance decomposition for empirical risk minimization.
Approximation error. By Proposition A.1, for any \(\delta > 0\) there exists a network \(G^*_n \in \mathcal{G}_n\) (for \(n\) large enough) with \(\sup_{\tau,x} |G^*_n(\tau,x) - Q^*(\tau, x)| < \delta\). The \(\beta\)-Holder assumption combined with the approximation rates of Schmidt-Hieber (2020) shows that \(\inf_{G \in \mathcal{G}_n} \|G - Q^*\|_\infty = O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d+1)})\) when the network architecture is chosen to balance approximation and estimation.
Estimation error. Define the integrated quantile loss \(L(G) = \int_0^1 \rho_\tau(y - G(\tau,x))\,d\tau\). By the Lipschitz property of \(\rho_\tau\) (used in Theorem A.3), \(L\) is Lipschitz in \(G\). The Rademacher complexity of the function class \(\{x \mapsto L(G(x)) : G \in \mathcal{G}_n\}\) is bounded by \(O(\sqrt{L_n W_n \log(L_n W_n) / n})\) via Lipschitz composition and the covering number bounds for ReLU networks (Padilla, Tansey, and Chen 2022, Theorem 2). The condition \(L_n W_n \log(L_n W_n) = o(n/\log n)\) ensures this vanishes.
Combining. Let \(R(G) = \mathbb{E}[L(G)]\) denote the population risk, \(\hat{R}_n(G) = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n L(G(X_i, Y_i))\) the empirical risk, and \(R^* = \inf_G R(G)\) the Bayes risk. Then \[
\begin{aligned}
R(\hat{G}_n) - R^* &\leq \underbrace{[R(\hat{G}_n) - \hat{R}_n(\hat{G}_n)]}_{\text{estimation}} + \underbrace{[\hat{R}_n(\hat{G}_n) - \hat{R}_n(G^*_n)]}_{\leq\, 0} \\
&\quad + \underbrace{[\hat{R}_n(G^*_n) - R(G^*_n)]}_{\text{estimation}} + \underbrace{[R(G^*_n) - R^*]}_{\text{approximation}}.
\end{aligned}
\] The second term is non-positive by definition of \(\hat{G}_n\) as the empirical risk minimizer. The first and third terms vanish by uniform convergence (Rademacher complexity bound). The fourth term vanishes by the approximation rate. Since \(\mathrm{CRPS}(G, y) = 2L(G) + \text{const}(y)\) by Theorem A.3, convergence of the population risk \(R\) implies convergence of the expected CRPS. \(\square\)
A practical concern is that the learned quantile function \(\hat{G}_n(\tau, x)\) may not be monotone in \(\tau\), leading to quantile crossing: \(\hat{G}_n(\tau_1, x) > \hat{G}_n(\tau_2, x)\) for some \(\tau_1 < \tau_2\). Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val, and Galichon (2010) showed that non-crossing can be enforced by post-processing:






TipProposition A.2: Rearrangement Eliminates Crossing



Let \(\hat{G}(\tau, x)\) be any (possibly crossing) quantile estimator. Define its non-decreasing rearrangement \(\hat{G}^{\uparrow}(\tau, x) = \inf\{y : \lambda\{s \in [0,1] : \hat{G}(s, x) \leq y\} \geq \tau\}\), where \(\lambda\) denotes Lebesgue measure. Then \(\hat{G}^{\uparrow}(\cdot, x)\) is non-decreasing and satisfies \[
\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(y - \hat{G}^{\uparrow}(\tau, x))\,d\tau \leq \int_0^1 \rho_\tau(y - \hat{G}(\tau, x))\,d\tau
\] for every \(y\). The rearranged estimator has lower integrated pinball loss than the original.


In practice, the IQN architecture with cosine embedding and the pinball loss rarely produces significant crossing, because the cosine embedding encourages smooth variation in \(\tau\) and the pinball loss penalizes crossing indirectly. When crossing does occur, the rearrangement above provides a simple fix.
Combining the approximation and estimation bounds yields an explicit convergence rate for the IQN estimator.






TipCorollary A.2: Convergence Rate of the IQN Estimator



Under the assumptions of Theorem A.4, if the network class \(\mathcal{G}_n\) has depth \(L_n = O(\log n)\) and width \(W_n = O(n^{(d+1)/(2(2\beta+d+1))})\), then \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(Y - \hat{G}_n(\tau, X))\,d\tau\right] - R^* = O\!\left(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + d + 1)} \log^2 n\right).
\] Equivalently, the expected CRPS satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CRPS}(\hat{G}_n, Y)] - \mathrm{CRPS}(Q^*, Y) = O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d+1)} \log^2 n)\). (The \(\log^2 n\) factor inherits from the \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) terms in the approximation bound of Theorem A.2 and the covering number bound; it is omitted in the simplified rates elsewhere in the book.)


The exponent \(d+1\) (rather than \(d\)) reflects the fact that the quantile function \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) lives on the \((d+1)\)-dimensional domain \([0,1] \times \mathcal{X}\), with \(\tau\) contributing one additional dimension. In practice, the \(\tau\)-direction is often smoother than the \(x\)-directions (the quantile function varies smoothly across quantile levels for continuous distributions), so this worst-case rate may be conservative.
Corollary A.2 gives the IQN convergence rate \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d+1)}\), which treats \(\tau\) as an additional input dimension. Theorem A.6 below gives the minimax lower bound \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}\) for estimating the quantile function in \(d\) covariates. The IQN rate is thus slightly slower than the minimax bound, by the factor accounting for \(\tau\) as an extra dimension. Whether an IQN can achieve the minimax rate \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}\) — by exploiting the known smoothness of \(Q^*\) in \(\tau\) rather than treating \(\tau\) as a full dimension — is an open question. Padilla, Tansey, and Chen (2022) establish the minimax rate for fixed-\(\tau\) quantile regression with ReLU networks but do not address the joint estimation over \(\tau\); closing this gap is an interesting direction for future work.
Consistency of the quantile estimator has direct implications for prediction interval coverage. If \(\hat{G}_n(\alpha/2, x)\) and \(\hat{G}_n(1 - \alpha/2, x)\) converge uniformly to \(Q^*(\alpha/2, x)\) and \(Q^*(1-\alpha/2, x)\), then the prediction interval \([\hat{G}_n(\alpha/2, x), \hat{G}_n(1 - \alpha/2, x)]\) achieves asymptotically correct coverage: \[
P\!\left(Y \in [\hat{G}_n(\alpha/2, X), \, \hat{G}_n(1 - \alpha/2, X)]\right) \to 1 - \alpha \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\] This holds because the event \(Y \in [Q^*(\alpha/2, x), Q^*(1-\alpha/2, x)]\) has probability exactly \(1 - \alpha\) by definition of the conditional quantiles, and the uniform convergence of \(\hat{G}_n\) to \(Q^*\) implies convergence of the coverage probability. For finite-sample coverage guarantees, the conformal calibration methods developed in Chapter 14 provide a complementary approach.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
section: A.4 CRPS Convergence of the IQN
text:
A.4 CRPS Convergence of the IQN
The consistency result in Theorem A.4 establishes convergence of the integrated pinball loss, which is a population-level risk. In practice, we care about the CRPS of our learned model on new observations — that is, we want the full predictive distribution produced by the IQN to converge to the true conditional distribution, not just in terms of a training objective but in terms of the distributional scoring rule that practitioners actually report. The following theorem makes this connection precise by showing that uniform convergence of the pinball loss over quantile levels implies convergence of the CRPS.
The CRPS is an integral of the pinball loss over \(\tau \in (0,1)\). If the IQN minimizes the pinball loss uniformly well for every quantile level — not just on average over randomly sampled \(\tau\) values — then the integrated loss (which is the CRPS up to a factor of 2) must also converge. This is a stronger statement than Theorem A.4, which only requires convergence of the average integrated loss. The upgrade from average to uniform convergence requires a covering argument over the quantile index \(\tau\).






TipTheorem A.5: CRPS Convergence of the IQN



Under the assumptions of Theorem A.4, suppose additionally that the conditional density \(f_{Y|X}(y|x)\) is bounded above by \(\bar{f} < \infty\) and bounded below by \(\underline{f} > 0\) on the support of \(Y\) given \(X\). Then the IQN estimator \(\hat{G}_n\) satisfies \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{CRPS}(\hat{G}_n, Y) - \mathrm{CRPS}(Q^*, Y)\right] = O\!\left(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + d + 1)} \log^2 n\right),
\] where the expectation is over both the training data and a new observation \((X, Y)\).


Proof. We proceed in three steps: discretization over \(\tau\), uniform convergence at a finite grid, and integration.
Step 1: Discretization. Fix \(\delta > 0\) and let \(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_K\) be a uniform grid on \((0,1)\) with spacing \(\delta\), so \(K = \lceil 1/\delta \rceil\). For any quantile function \(G\), the integrated pinball loss can be approximated by its Riemann sum: \[
\left|\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(y - G(\tau,x))\,d\tau - \delta\sum_{k=1}^K \rho_{\tau_k}(y - G(\tau_k, x))\right| \leq \delta \cdot \omega_G(\delta),
\] where \(\omega_G(\delta) = \sup_{|\tau - \tau'| \leq \delta} |G(\tau, x) - G(\tau', x)|\) is the modulus of continuity of \(G\) in \(\tau\). For the true quantile function \(Q^*\), the bounded density assumption implies \(\omega_{Q^*}(\delta) \leq \delta / \underline{f}\), so the Riemann approximation error is \(O(\delta^2)\).
Step 2: Uniform convergence at fixed \(\tau\). For each fixed \(\tau_k\), the pointwise pinball loss minimizer over \(\mathcal{G}_n\) converges at the rate established in Theorem A.4. To handle all \(K\) grid points simultaneously, we apply a union bound. The Rademacher complexity bound from the consistency proof gives, for each \(\tau_k\), \[
\sup_{G \in \mathcal{G}_n} \left|\hat{R}_n^\tau(G) - R^\tau(G)\right| = O_p\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{L_n W_n \log(L_n W_n)}{n}}\right),
\] where \(R^\tau(G) = \mathbb{E}[\rho_\tau(Y - G(\tau, X))]\) and \(\hat{R}_n^\tau\) is its empirical counterpart. Since the bound does not depend on \(\tau\), uniform convergence over the grid follows immediately — no union bound penalty is needed. The empirical minimizer at each grid point converges to the population minimizer \(Q^*(\tau_k, \cdot)\) at the same rate as in Corollary A.2.
Step 3: Integration. Combining Steps 1 and 2, we have \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CRPS}(\hat{G}_n, Y)] - \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CRPS}(Q^*, Y)]
&= 2\int_0^1 \left[\mathbb{E}[\rho_\tau(Y - \hat{G}_n(\tau, X))] - \mathbb{E}[\rho_\tau(Y - Q^*(\tau, X))]\right]d\tau \\
&\leq 2\int_0^1 \sup_x |R^\tau(\hat{G}_n) - R^\tau(Q^*)|\,d\tau.
\end{aligned}
\] By the Lipschitz bound on \(\rho_\tau\) and the \(\varepsilon\)-approximation guarantee, the integrand at each \(\tau\) is bounded by the approximation error plus the estimation error. Since both are \(O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d+1)})\) uniformly in \(\tau\) (the approximation rate from Theorem A.2 holds uniformly and the Rademacher bound is \(\tau\)-independent), the integral inherits the same rate. \(\square\)
The practical implication of Theorem A.5 is reassuring. When we train an IQN by sampling random \(\tau\) values during each SGD step, the stochastic approximation to the integral \(\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(\cdot)\,d\tau\) converges to the true integral by the law of large numbers over training iterations. The theorem then guarantees that the resulting CRPS on held-out data converges to the CRPS of the oracle quantile function at a quantifiable rate. This is the sense in which the IQN is a consistent distributional estimator, not merely a consistent point estimator.
What does the bounded density assumption buy us? Without the lower bound \(\underline{f} > 0\), the quantile function \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) could have vertical segments (flat regions in the CDF correspond to jumps in the quantile function), making the Riemann approximation in Step 1 arbitrarily poor. The upper bound \(\bar{f} < \infty\) ensures that the quantile function is Lipschitz in \(\tau\), which controls the approximation error in the \(\tau\)-direction separately from the \(x\)-direction. For distributions with atoms or unbounded densities, the CRPS convergence still holds but at a potentially slower rate that depends on the regularity of the quantile function near the boundary.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
text:
A.5 Minimax Rates
The minimax rate characterizes the best possible convergence speed, uniformly over a function class. For quantile regression with ReLU networks, Padilla, Tansey, and Chen (2022) establish the following.






TipTheorem A.6: Minimax Rate for Quantile Regression with ReLU Networks



Let \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) be \(\beta\)-Holder smooth in \(x \in [0,1]^d\) for each \(\tau \in (0,1)\), with \(\beta > 0\). The minimax rate for estimating \(Q^*\) from \(n\) i.i.d. observations \((X_i, Y_i)_{i=1}^n\) is \[
\inf_{\hat{Q}} \sup_{Q^* \in \mathcal{H}(\beta, d)} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_0^1 \rho_\tau(Y - \hat{Q}(\tau, X))\,d\tau\right] \asymp n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + d)},
\] where the infimum is over all estimators and \(\mathcal{H}(\beta, d)\) is the \(\beta\)-Holder class on \([0,1]^d\). A ReLU network with \(O(n^{d/(2\beta+d)})\) parameters and depth \(O(\log n)\) achieves this rate.


The rate \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}\) reveals the curse of dimensionality: as \(d\) grows, convergence slows dramatically. For \(\beta = 2\) and \(d = 20\), the rate is \(n^{-1/6} \approx n^{-0.17}\). This motivates the compositional approach developed in the next section.
For kernel-based quantile regression (e.g., Nadaraya–Watson), the minimax rate is also \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}\) when the function is merely Holder smooth. The rates coincide for flat (non-compositional) function classes. The advantage of neural networks emerges only when the target function has additional structure, as we discuss next.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
text:
A.6 Compositional Structure and Depth
The theoretical advantage of deep networks over kernel methods is their ability to exploit compositional structure. The quantile transport map naturally possesses this structure when the conditional distribution depends on \(x\) through a lower-dimensional summary.






TipDefinition A.1: Compositional Structure



A function \(Q : [0,1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) has compositional structure with intrinsic dimension \(k\) if \[
Q(\tau, x) = g(\tau, f(x)),
\tag{A.1}\] where \(f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k\) is a feature map with \(k \ll d\), and \(g : [0,1] \times \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}\) is the reduced quantile function.


This structure arises naturally in several GBC settings. When \(S(Z_{1:n})\) is a \(k\)-dimensional sufficient statistic, the predictive quantile function depends on the data only through \(S\) (see Chapter 11), so the map \(f\) is simply the sufficient summary. When a neural network learns to compress inputs into a bottleneck layer of dimension \(k\), the post-bottleneck layers implement \(g\), with the bottleneck itself serving as \(f\). And when the response depends on a few combinations of the inputs — for example, the radial distance \(r = \|x\|\) in a rotationally symmetric problem — \(f\) captures those combinations and \(g\) maps them to quantile predictions.






TipTheorem A.7: Minimax Rate for Compositional Quantile Functions



Let \(Q(\tau, x) = g(\tau, f(x))\) as in Eq. A.1, where \(f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k\) and \(g : [0,1] \times \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}\) are each \(\beta\)-Holder smooth. A ReLU network estimator \(\hat{Q}\) with depth \(O(\log n)\) achieves \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_0^1 \int |\hat{Q}(\tau, s) - Q(\tau, s)|^2 \, dP_S(s)\, d\tau\right] = O\!\left(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + k + 1)}\right),
\] where \(P_S\) is the distribution of \(S = f(X)\) and the rate depends on \(k\) (the intrinsic dimension), not \(d\) (the ambient dimension).


Proof sketch. The argument, following Schmidt-Hieber (2020) and Montanelli and Yang (2020), proceeds in two steps.
Step 1: Layer-wise approximation. The network allocates its initial layers to approximating \(f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k\) and its final layers to approximating \(g : [0,1] \times \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}\). Each component is a function on a domain of dimension at most \(\max(d, k+1)\), but the critical observation is that the estimation complexity is governed by the lower-dimensional component. The first layers learn \(f\) from the full \(d\)-dimensional input, but \(f\) is a fixed map that needs to be learned only once. The stochastic component — the quantile variation in \(\tau\) — operates in the \((k+1)\)-dimensional space \([0,1] \times \mathbb{R}^k\).
Step 2: Rate calculation. The approximation error for \(g\) on \([0,1] \times \mathbb{R}^k\) scales as \(O(N_g^{-2\beta/(k+1)})\) where \(N_g\) is the number of parameters allocated to approximating \(g\). The estimation error (via Rademacher complexity) scales as \(O(\sqrt{N_g \log N_g / n})\). Balancing gives \(N_g \asymp n^{(k+1)/(2\beta+k+1)}\) and the overall rate \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+k+1)}\). \(\square\)
The improvement from exploiting compositional structure can be dramatic:



Table A.1: Convergence rates for different estimators and effective dimensions.
