When the intrinsic dimension \(k\) is small, the neural network rate is vastly superior to the kernel rate. This explains the empirical success of IQN on high-dimensional problems with underlying low-dimensional structure.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
section: A.7 Minimax Rate Proof Sketches for Deep Compositional Networks
text:
A.7 Minimax Rate Proof Sketches for Deep Compositional Networks
The rates in Theorem A.7 are consequences of a deeper result about how deep ReLU networks achieve minimax-optimal approximation for smooth functions of smooth functions. We sketch the three key steps of the argument here, following Schmidt-Hieber (2020) and Montanelli and Yang (2020), because the ideas illuminate why depth is essential and why shallow methods cannot match these rates.
The setting is the following. Suppose the target function has a multi-level compositional structure \(Q = g_L \circ g_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ g_1\), where each \(g_\ell : \mathbb{R}^{d_\ell} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell+1}}\) is \(\beta\)-Holder smooth and the intermediate dimensions \(d_\ell\) are small. For the quantile transport map, a natural two-level composition is \(Q(\tau, x) = g(\tau, f(x))\) with \(g_1 = f\) and \(g_2 = g\), but the argument extends to arbitrary depth.
Step (a): Approximation theory for compositions. The core observation is that a deep ReLU network can approximate a composition \(g_L \circ \cdots \circ g_1\) by allocating separate blocks of layers to each component \(g_\ell\). A standard ReLU network with \(O(\varepsilon^{-d_\ell/\beta})\) parameters can approximate a \(\beta\)-smooth function \(g_\ell : \mathbb{R}^{d_\ell} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell+1}}\) to within \(\varepsilon\) in the supremum norm (Theorem A.2). When the components are stacked, the errors compose: if \(g_\ell\) is approximated to within \(\varepsilon_\ell\), the overall error is controlled by \(\sum_\ell C_\ell \varepsilon_\ell\) where \(C_\ell\) depends on the Lipschitz constants of the subsequent layers. The total number of parameters is \(\sum_\ell O(\varepsilon_\ell^{-d_\ell/\beta})\), and optimizing over the allocation of accuracy across layers gives a total parameter count that depends on \(\max_\ell d_\ell\) rather than the ambient input dimension \(d\). This is the approximation-theoretic mechanism by which depth breaks the curse of dimensionality. A shallow network, by contrast, must approximate the composed function monolithically, paying the full \(O(\varepsilon^{-d/\beta})\) cost.
Step (b): Covering number bounds. To convert approximation rates into estimation rates, we need to control the complexity of the network class. The \(\varepsilon\)-covering number \(\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon, \mathcal{G}(L, W, S), \|\cdot\|_\infty)\) of a ReLU network class with depth \(L\), width \(W\), and \(S\) total parameters satisfies \[
\log \mathcal{N}(\varepsilon, \mathcal{G}(L, W, S), \|\cdot\|_\infty) \leq C \cdot S \cdot L \cdot \log(W / \varepsilon)
\tag{A.2}\] for a universal constant \(C\). This bound, due to Bartlett et al. (2019), is the sharpest available and is crucial because it scales linearly in the number of parameters \(S\) rather than exponentially in the depth \(L\). The linear scaling ensures that deeper networks do not automatically incur a heavier statistical penalty. The factor of \(L\) in the bound reflects the fact that deeper networks can represent sharper functions (the Lipschitz constant grows exponentially with depth in the worst case), but for the compositional architectures we consider, the Lipschitz constant of each layer is bounded, keeping the overall covering number under control.
Step (c): Oracle inequality. The final step combines Steps (a) and (b) into an oracle inequality. Define the excess risk \(\mathcal{E}(\hat{G}_n) = R(\hat{G}_n) - R^*\), where \(R\) is the population integrated pinball loss. The standard empirical process bound gives \[
\mathcal{E}(\hat{G}_n) \leq \underbrace{\inf_{G \in \mathcal{G}_n} R(G) - R^*}_{\text{approximation}} + \underbrace{C' \sqrt{\frac{S_n L_n \log(W_n n)}{n}}}_{\text{estimation}}.
\] For a compositional target with intrinsic dimensions \((d_1, d_2)\) and a two-level network architecture, the approximation term from Step (a) gives \(O(N^{-2\beta/\max(d_1, d_2)})\) where \(N = S_n\) is the total parameter count. The estimation term from Step (b) gives \(O(\sqrt{N \log N / n})\). Balancing these two contributions by choosing \(N \asymp n^{\max(d_1,d_2)/(2\beta + \max(d_1,d_2))}\) yields the oracle rate \[
\mathcal{E}(\hat{G}_n) = O\!\left(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + \max(d_1, d_2))}\right).
\] For the quantile transport map \(Q(\tau, x) = g(\tau, f(x))\) with \(d_1 = d\) (ambient) and \(d_2 = k + 1\) (intrinsic plus \(\tau\)), the rate becomes \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + k + 1)}\) whenever \(k + 1 < d\), recovering Theorem A.6. The point is that the estimation rate is governed by the bottleneck dimension \(\max(d_1, d_2)\), but since \(f\) is deterministic (no stochastic component), the effective bottleneck is \(d_2 = k + 1\), not \(d_1 = d\). (This assumes the neural network architecture correctly identifies the intrinsic dimension \(k\); estimating \(f\) from data still incurs cost in the ambient dimension \(d\) unless the architecture imposes the low-dimensional structure explicitly, as in Schmidt-Hieber (2020) Theorem 1.)
The oracle inequality also reveals why naive application of neural networks without compositional structure gives no advantage over kernels. If the network is a single monolithic block approximating \(Q\) on \([0,1]^{d+1}\), both the approximation and estimation terms scale with the full dimension \(d+1\), and the resulting rate \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d+1)}\) matches the kernel rate (up to the extra +1 from the \(\tau\) dimension). The advantage of depth is not automatic — it requires the target to have compositional structure, and the architecture to mirror that structure through appropriate layer allocation.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
section: A.8 Autoregressive Noise Outsourcing for Multivariate \(\theta\)
text:
A.8 Autoregressive Noise Outsourcing for Multivariate \(\theta\)
The noise outsourcing theorem (Chapter 4, Theorem 4.1) establishes that any univariate conditional distribution can be represented as a deterministic function of a single uniform random variable and the conditioning variable. In Bayesian inference, however, we frequently encounter multi-dimensional parameter vectors \(\theta = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d)\) with correlated posterior components. The question is whether the univariate machinery extends to this setting, and whether the resulting generator recovers the full joint posterior \(\pi(\theta | y)\). The answer is affirmative, and the mechanism is the autoregressive decomposition introduced in Chapter 4 (Theorem 4.3). Here we provide the formal proof that this decomposition is exact — that it recovers the joint posterior without any approximation error from the decomposition itself.
The proof uses the chain rule of conditional distributions to factor the joint density into a product of univariate conditionals, then applies the univariate noise outsourcing theorem to each conditional in the factorization.






TipTheorem A.8: Autoregressive Noise Outsourcing for the Joint Posterior



Let \(\pi(\theta | y)\) be the posterior distribution of \(\theta = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) given data \(y \in \mathcal{Y}\), and assume \(\pi(\theta | y)\) admits a density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) for almost every \(y\). Then there exist measurable functions \(G_1^*, G_2^*, \ldots, G_d^*\) such that \[
\begin{aligned}
\theta_1 &= G_1^*(\tau_1, y), \\
\theta_2 &= G_2^*(\tau_2, y, \theta_1), \\
&\;\;\vdots \\
\theta_d &= G_d^*(\tau_d, y, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{d-1}),
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.3}\] where \(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_d \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) are jointly independent of \(y\), and each \(G_j^*\) is the conditional quantile function \[
G_j^*(\tau, y, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}) = F_{\theta_j | \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}, y}^{-1}(\tau).
\tag{A.4}\] The resulting random vector \((\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d)\) has distribution \(\pi(\theta | y)\).


Proof. We proceed by induction on \(d\), using the chain rule of conditional distributions and the univariate noise outsourcing theorem at each step.
Base case (\(d = 1\)). The marginal posterior \(\pi(\theta_1 | y)\) is a univariate distribution. By the univariate noise outsourcing theorem (Theorem 4.1 in Chapter 4), there exists a measurable function \(G_1^* : [0,1] \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\theta_1 = G_1^*(\tau_1, y)\) with \(\tau_1 \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) independent of \(y\), and \(G_1^*(\cdot, y) = F_{\theta_1 | y}^{-1}(\cdot)\) is the quantile function of \(\pi(\theta_1 | y)\).
Inductive step. Suppose that the first \(j-1\) components have been generated as \(\theta_k = G_k^*(\tau_k, y, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{k-1})\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, j-1\), using independent uniforms \(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_{j-1}\), and that the resulting \((\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1})\) has distribution \(\pi(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1} | y)\). We need to generate \(\theta_j\) from the conditional \(\pi(\theta_j | \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}, y)\).
Conditioned on \(y\) and the realized values \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}\), the distribution \(\pi(\theta_j | \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}, y)\) is a univariate distribution on \(\mathbb{R}\). By the univariate noise outsourcing theorem applied to this conditional distribution, there exists a measurable function \(G_j^*\) such that \[
\theta_j = G_j^*(\tau_j, y, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1})
\] with \(\tau_j \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) independent of \((y, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1})\). Since \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}\) are deterministic functions of \((\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_{j-1}, y)\), the independence of \(\tau_j\) from \((y, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1})\) is equivalent to the independence of \(\tau_j\) from \((\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_{j-1}, y)\), which holds by construction since \(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_d\) are i.i.d.
Verifying the joint distribution. By the chain rule of conditional distributions, \[
\pi(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d | y) = \pi(\theta_1 | y) \cdot \pi(\theta_2 | \theta_1, y) \cdots \pi(\theta_d | \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{d-1}, y).
\tag{A.5}\] The construction generates \(\theta_j\) from precisely the \(j\)-th factor \(\pi(\theta_j | \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}, y)\) in this product, using an independent uniform \(\tau_j\). To verify that the joint distribution is correct, compute the probability of any event \(A = A_1 \times \cdots \times A_d \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\): \[
\begin{aligned}
P(\theta \in A \mid y) &= P(\theta_1 \in A_1 \mid y) \cdot P(\theta_2 \in A_2 \mid \theta_1, y) \cdots P(\theta_d \in A_d \mid \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{d-1}, y) \\
&= \int_{A_1} \pi(\theta_1 \mid y)\,d\theta_1 \cdot \int_{A_2} \pi(\theta_2 \mid \theta_1, y)\,d\theta_2 \cdots \int_{A_d} \pi(\theta_d \mid \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{d-1}, y)\,d\theta_d \\
&= \int_{A_1 \times \cdots \times A_d} \pi(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d \mid y)\,d\theta_1 \cdots d\theta_d,
\end{aligned}
\] which is precisely the probability assigned by the joint posterior \(\pi(\theta | y)\). Since this holds for all product sets \(A\) (which generate the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}^d\)), the distribution of \((\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d)\) equals \(\pi(\theta | y)\). \(\square\)
First, the decomposition is exact — no approximation is introduced by the autoregressive factorization. The only source of error in the GBC pipeline is the neural network approximation of each conditional quantile function \(G_j^*\), and this error is controlled by the consistency results of Theorem A.4. Second, the ordering of the components \((\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d)\) is arbitrary: any permutation gives a valid decomposition. However, some orderings lead to simpler conditional quantile functions than others, which affects the ease of learning. In practice, ordering components so that the most informative (most constrained by the data) component comes first tends to simplify the subsequent conditionals.
Third, the proof reveals why independent uniform draws suffice to generate correlated posterior draws. The correlation between \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) is not encoded in any dependence between \(\tau_1\) and \(\tau_2\) (which are independent by construction), but rather in the function \(G_2^*(\tau_2, y, \theta_1)\), which depends on the already-generated value \(\theta_1\). A different value of \(\theta_1\) leads to a different conditional distribution \(\pi(\theta_2 | \theta_1, y)\), and hence to a different quantile function \(G_2^*(\cdot, y, \theta_1)\). The dependence structure is captured entirely by the conditioning structure of the quantile functions, not by the noise inputs.
Finally, combining Theorem A.8 with the CRPS convergence result (Theorem A.5) gives an end-to-end guarantee for multi-parameter posterior inference. If each conditional quantile function \(G_j^*\) is learned by an IQN that achieves CRPS convergence at rate \(O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + k_j + 1)})\), where \(k_j\) is the effective conditioning dimension for the \(j\)-th conditional, then the total variation distance between the generated joint posterior and the true joint posterior converges to zero as the training data increase. The rate for the joint posterior is governed by the slowest-converging conditional, which is the one with the largest effective dimension \(k_j\).

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
text:
A.9 Barron’s Spectral Bound
An alternative route to dimension-free approximation rates, due to Barron (1993), avoids Holder smoothness entirely and instead assumes a spectral condition on the target function.






TipTheorem A.9: Barron’s Bound



Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) have finite first moment of the Fourier magnitude distribution: \[
C_f = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \|\omega\| \, |\hat{f}(\omega)|\, d\omega < \infty.
\] Then for any \(m \geq 1\), there exists a single-hidden-layer sigmoidal network with \(m\) hidden units such that \[
\int |f(x) - h_m(x)|^2 \, d\mu(x) \leq \frac{C_f^2}{m},
\] where \(\mu\) is any probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). The rate \(O(1/m)\) is independent of \(d\).


The approximation rate depends on the spectral complexity \(C_f\), not the input dimension \(d\). For quantile functions \(Q^*(\tau, x)\) that are smooth in both \(\tau\) and \(x\), the Fourier condition is satisfied with \(C_{Q^*}\) depending on the smoothness but not on \(d\). This provides a complementary explanation for why neural networks avoid the curse of dimensionality — not through compositional structure, but through spectral regularity.
N. Polson and Sokolov (2020) discuss Barron’s bound in the context of deep learning and show that depth amplifies this effect: deep networks can approximate compositions of Barron-class functions with rates that are multiplicative rather than additive in the component complexities.
The compositional structure of deep networks has a classical antecedent in the Kolmogorov–Arnold superposition theorem (1957), which states that any continuous function \(f : [0,1]^d \to \mathbb{R}\) can be written as \[
f(x_1, \ldots, x_d) = \sum_{q=0}^{2d} \Phi_q\!\left(\sum_{p=1}^{d} \phi_{q,p}(x_p)\right),
\] where \(\phi_{q,p} : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(\Phi_q : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) are continuous functions. This is a two-layer composition with univariate inner functions and a univariate outer function.
Montanelli and Yang (2020) use this representation to derive approximation bounds for deep ReLU networks. Their key result is that a ReLU network of depth \(O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) can approximate any function in the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation to within \(\varepsilon\), with the number of parameters scaling polynomially in \(1/\varepsilon\) and independently of \(d\) (up to the \(2d+1\) outer sums). This provides yet another route — beyond Holder smoothness and Barron’s spectral condition — through which deep networks escape the curse of dimensionality.
For the quantile transport map \(Q^*(\tau, x)\), the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation applies with \(p = d + 1\) (treating \(\tau\) as one of the inputs). The inner functions \(\phi_{q,p}\) can be interpreted as learned feature extractors that reduce each input coordinate to a one-dimensional summary, while the outer functions \(\Phi_q\) combine these summaries into the quantile prediction. This resonates with the IQN architecture, where the cosine embedding acts as the \(\tau\)-branch feature extractor and the elementwise product combines the \(\tau\) and \(x\) features before the outer layers.
When the quantile network is embedded in a Bayesian framework with a sparsity-inducing prior on the weights, N. G. Polson and Ročková (2018) establish posterior concentration rates. Specifically, if the prior assigns exponentially small probability to networks with more than \(s\) active parameters and the true function lies in a \(\beta\)-Holder ball, the posterior concentrates at the minimax rate \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}\) (or the compositional rate when structure is present). This provides a Bayesian justification for the frequentist minimax rates above and connects the GBC framework to the broader program of Bayesian nonparametrics.

title: Appendix A — Proofs and Convergence Theory
section: A.10 Summary of the Theoretical Chain
text:
A.10 Summary of the Theoretical Chain
The results in this appendix fit together as a logical chain that supports the GBC framework end to end. We summarize the chain here.
Existence. The noise outsourcing theorem (Theorem 4.1 in Chapter 4) guarantees that for any joint distribution \((X, Y)\), there exists a measurable function \(Q^*(\tau, x) = F_{Y|X}^{-1}(\tau \mid x)\) such that \(Y = Q^*(U, X)\) with \(U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) independent of \(X\). The function \(Q^*\) is the conditional quantile function and encodes the full conditional distribution.
Representability. Theorems A.1–A.2 and Proposition A.1 guarantee that \(Q^*\) can be approximated to arbitrary accuracy by a neural network — including the specific IQN architecture with cosine embedding. The approximation error vanishes as the network grows.
Training objective. Theorem A.3 shows that the pinball loss controls the CRPS: if the quantile approximation is \(\varepsilon\)-accurate, the CRPS error is at most \(2\varepsilon\). The integrated pinball loss over uniform \(\tau\) is equivalent to the Wasserstein-1 distance between the learned and true conditional distributions (Corollary A.1). Minimizing the pinball loss is therefore equivalent to minimizing a distributional distance.
Consistency. Theorem A.4 establishes that the empirical risk minimizer \(\hat{G}_n\) converges to \(Q^*\) as the sample size \(n \to \infty\), provided the network class grows at an appropriate rate. The CRPS of the learned model converges to the CRPS of the true conditional distribution.
CRPS convergence. Theorem A.5 strengthens the consistency result by showing that the CRPS convergence holds uniformly over quantile levels, not just on average. The CRPS gap between the IQN and the oracle vanishes at the rate \(O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d+1)})\), ensuring that the full predictive distribution improves as training data grow.
Optimal rates. Theorem A.6 gives the minimax rate \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}\) for \(\beta\)-Holder smooth quantile functions, which ReLU networks achieve. Theorem A.7 shows that when the quantile function has compositional structure with intrinsic dimension \(k \ll d\), the rate improves to \(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+k+1)}\), escaping the curse of dimensionality. The proof sketches in Section A.7 detail the three-step argument — approximation of compositions, covering number bounds, and oracle inequality — that establishes these rates. Barron’s bound (Theorem A.9) provides a complementary dimension-free rate under spectral regularity.
Multivariate parameters. Theorem A.8 proves that the autoregressive noise outsourcing decomposition recovers the exact joint posterior \(\pi(\theta | y)\) for \(d\)-dimensional parameter vectors, using \(d\) independent uniform draws and \(d\) conditional quantile functions. The proof applies the univariate noise outsourcing theorem iteratively via the chain rule of conditional distributions, and the resulting generator captures all posterior correlations through the conditioning structure of the quantile functions.
Practical implication. Taken together, these results justify the GBC pipeline: train an IQN on i.i.d. data by minimizing the pinball loss, and the resulting model provably converges to the true conditional quantile function at an optimal rate that depends on the intrinsic complexity of the problem, not the ambient dimension. For multi-parameter posteriors, the autoregressive extension guarantees exact joint distribution recovery, with each conditional quantile function enjoying its own consistency and rate guarantees.
Bibliographic notes. The universal approximation theorem was established independently by Hornik, Stinchcombe, and White (1989) and Cybenko (1989). Deep ReLU approximation rates were developed by Schmidt-Hieber (2020), with extensions to compositional functions by Montanelli and Yang (2020). The Barron spectral bound appears in Barron (1993); N. Polson and Sokolov (2020) provide a modern treatment in the deep learning context. Quantile regression was introduced by Koenker and Bassett (1978); minimax rates for quantile regression with neural networks are due to Padilla, Tansey, and Chen (2022). The CRPS–pinball equivalence is established in Gneiting and Raftery (2007). Covering number bounds for deep networks are developed by Bartlett et al. (2019). Posterior concentration for deep networks with sparsity priors is treated by N. G. Polson and Ročková (2018). The non-crossing rearrangement for quantile estimators is due to Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val, and Galichon (2010). White (1992) provides early results on nonparametric quantile estimation with neural networks. The autoregressive decomposition for multivariate generative models is standard in the deep learning literature; our formulation follows the noise outsourcing framework of Kallenberg (1997).

title: Appendix B — Computing Environment
text:
B.2 PyTorch and GPU Setup
GBC models train comfortably on a CPU for the pedagogical examples in Chapters 3 through 5 (each runs in under a minute). For the larger experiments in Chapters 7 through 9, a GPU reduces wall-clock time from minutes to seconds.
CUDA (NVIDIA GPUs). Install the CUDA-enabled build of PyTorch following the instructions at pytorch.org/get-started. The exact command depends on your CUDA toolkit version. For CUDA 12.1:
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121
For CUDA 12.4 (common on newer distributions and HPC nodes running the latest driver):
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124
Verify that CUDA is available:
import torch
print(torch.cuda.is_available())       # True
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))   # e.g. "NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB"
A common source of confusion is a mismatch between the CUDA toolkit version compiled into PyTorch and the driver version installed on the host. The PyTorch CUDA runtime is self-contained, so you do not need a system-wide CUDA installation — but the NVIDIA driver must be new enough to support the CUDA version. Run nvidia-smi at the command line to see the maximum CUDA version your driver supports, and make sure it is at least as high as the version in the pip install URL. If torch.cuda.is_available() returns False despite having an NVIDIA GPU, this version mismatch is the most likely culprit.
To move a model and its data to the GPU, use the .to() method on both:
device = torch.device("cuda")
model = IQN(xdim=1).to(device)
X_t = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32).to(device)
The train_het_mlp function accepts a device argument, so in practice we pass device=get_device() and the library handles placement automatically. The other training functions — train_iqn and train_classifier — always run on CPU (they have no device parameter). For large datasets that benefit from GPU acceleration, use the het-MLP pipeline.
Apple Silicon (MPS). On macOS with an M-series chip, PyTorch 2.0+ supports the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend:
import torch
print(torch.backends.mps.is_available())  # True on M1/M2/M3/M4
device = torch.device("mps")
MPS provides roughly 3–5\(\times\) speedup over CPU for the network sizes used in this book. All gbc code works on MPS without modification.
CPU fallback. If no GPU is available, every example still runs — it just takes longer. The gbc.utils.get_device() helper selects the best available backend automatically:
from gbc.utils import get_device
device = get_device()  # cuda > mps > cpu
Reproducibility across devices. Neural network training is not bitwise reproducible across devices (CPU vs. CUDA vs. MPS) because floating-point operations are reordered for performance. We fix random seeds via gbc.utils.set_seed() to make results reproducible on the same device. The numerical conclusions — CRPS, RMSE, coverage — are stable across platforms to within the reported standard errors.

title: Appendix B — Computing Environment
text:
B.3 The gbc Package
The book ships with a companion Python package called gbc. Every code listing in the chapters imports from this package rather than re-implementing algorithms from scratch. This keeps the chapter code focused on using the methods rather than defining them.
The gbc package is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/VadimSokolov/gbc. You can install it directly with pip:
pip install git+https://github.com/VadimSokolov/gbc.git
To follow along with the book examples and modify the source, clone and install in editable mode instead:
git clone https://github.com/VadimSokolov/gbc.git
cd gbc
pip install -e ".[dev]"
The -e (editable) flag means that changes to the source files take effect immediately without reinstalling.
The package is organized into the following modules:

B.3.1 Module API Reference
We provide a concise reference for the most important functions and classes in each module. Full docstrings are available via Python’s help() built-in.
gbc.iqn — the core of the book. IQN(xdim, hdim=256, nh=32) constructs the implicit quantile network with cosine tau-embedding. The forward(x, tau) method takes x, an (n, xdim) input tensor, and tau, a scalar float in (0, 1); pass different tau values to get different quantile predictions. It returns an (n, 2) tensor whose columns are the conditional mean and the quantile estimate at level tau. train_iqn(X, y, epochs=3000, hdim=256, nh=32, lr=1e-3, wd=1e-4, seed=42, w=(0.3, 0.3, 0.4)) handles full-batch Adam training with cosine annealing and returns a five-tuple (model, xm, xs, ym, ys) containing the trained model alongside the normalization statistics needed at test time. sample_iqn(model, X_te, xm, xs, ym, ys, B=500) sweeps 500 evenly-spaced quantile levels through the trained network and returns a (B, n_test) array of draws from the learned predictive distribution.
gbc.loss — three loss functions. pinball_loss(y, y_hat, tau) computes the standard check loss \(\rho_\tau(y - \hat{y})\). composite_loss(y, f, tau, w) combines an L1 anchor on the conditional mean, a monotonicity regularizer, and the pinball term with weights w. gaussian_nll(mu, logvar, y) provides the heteroscedastic Gaussian negative log-likelihood used by the HetMLP ensemble.
gbc.ensemble — the het-MLP ensemble from Chapter 14. HetMLP(xdim, hdim=256, nlayers=3) is a standard MLP with two output heads: one for the predicted mean and one for the log-variance. train_het_mlp(X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor, epochs=5000, hdim=256, nlayers=3, lr=1e-3, batch_size=8192, seed=42, device=None) trains a single member with mini-batch SGD. Note: X must be a PyTorch tensor (use torch.tensor(X_np, dtype=torch.float32) to convert from NumPy). ensemble_predict(models, X) aggregates predictions from a list of trained members using the law of total variance and returns (ens_mean, ens_std) arrays.
gbc.augment — the Aug-IQN pipeline from Chapter 8. em_labels(y, n_components=2, seed=42) clusters the response into regimes via a Gaussian mixture model. BoundaryClassifier(xdim, hdim=256, nlayers=3) and its companion train_classifier(X, labels, ...) learn a regime probability from the covariates. augment_features(X, classifier) appends the predicted regime probability as a (d+1)-th feature column, which is then passed to a standard IQN.
gbc.active_learning — the randomized-prior ensemble from Chapter 9. RandomPriorNet(xdim, hdim=128, nlayers=3, prior_scale=1.0) adds a frozen random network to a trainable network following Osband et al. (2018). ensemble_disagreement(models, X) returns the pointwise standard deviation across ensemble members. select_next(models, X_candidates, batch_size=1) picks the candidates with highest disagreement.
gbc.causal — the causal IQN from Chapter 13. CausalIQN(xdim=1, hsz=32, nh=32) has four sub-modules: a propensity network, a baseline-outcome network, a treatment-effect network, and a cosine tau-embedding. The .fit(x, y, z, epochs=3000, ...) method trains with a composite loss that includes a binary cross-entropy term on the propensity score. .estimate_cate(x, z, n_mc=500) sweeps random quantile levels through the treatment-effect head and returns the median as a point estimate alongside the full (n, n_mc) sample array. These samples are quantile treatment effects (QTEs), not the conditional mean \(E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X]\); the median QTE equals the conventional CATE only when the treatment-effect distribution is symmetric. Note that the z argument is passed to forward but does not affect the te head, so it has no effect on the returned values.
gbc.conformal — conformal prediction intervals from Chapter 14. temporal_cv_quantiles(residuals, strata, alpha=0.90, min_count=20) computes per-stratum quantiles from out-of-fold absolute residuals. conformal_pi(y_hat, strata, quantile_map) constructs symmetric prediction intervals centered on the point forecast.
gbc.metrics — we use five metrics throughout the book. crps_samples(y, samples) computes the energy-score estimator of the CRPS from a (B, n) array of predictive draws. crps_gaussian(y, mu, sigma) uses the closed-form expression for Gaussian forecasts. coverage(y, samples, alpha=0.90) and pi_width(samples, alpha=0.90) report empirical coverage and average interval width, respectively. rmse(y, y_hat) and rmspe(y, y_hat) round out the suite with point-forecast accuracy.
gbc.data — dataset loaders. load_motorcycle() returns the 133-row MASS::mcycle dataset as (X, y). friedman1(X) evaluates the Friedman #1 function. jump_fn(x) provides a 1D jump test function. make_bimodal(n, n_obs, theta_true, seed) generates the bimodal posterior ABC benchmark. lhs_1d(n, lo, hi, seed) produces a stratified 1D sample.
gbc.plotting — two workhorse plotting functions. quantile_fan(x, samples, ...) draws nested shaded prediction bands at multiple coverage levels with optional overlays for the true function and training data. calibration_plot(y, samples, ...) produces a PIT histogram that reveals whether the predictive distribution is calibrated. set_theme() applies the book’s standard figure style to all subsequent Matplotlib plots.
gbc.utils — three small helpers. set_seed(seed=42) sets seeds for PyTorch, NumPy, and CUDA. get_device() returns the best available torch.device (CUDA > CPU). cosine_schedule(optimizer, T_max, eta_min_ratio=0.01) wraps PyTorch’s CosineAnnealingLR scheduler.
A minimal example that trains an IQN on the motorcycle data:

Show code (9 lines)

#| eval: false
from gbc import IQN, train_iqn, sample_iqn
from gbc.data import load_motorcycle
from gbc.utils import set_seed, get_device

set_seed(42)
X, y = load_motorcycle()
model, xm, xs, ym, ys = train_iqn(X, y, epochs=2000, lr=1e-3)
samples = sample_iqn(model, X, xm, xs, ym, ys, B=200)

title: Appendix B — Computing Environment
text:
B.5 Reproducing Results
Every chapter in Parts II and III includes both pedagogical examples (which execute during the Quarto render) and full-scale experiments (which use cached results). Here we describe how to reproduce the cached results from scratch.
The pedagogical examples in Chapters 3–5 — 1D quantile regression, noise outsourcing demonstrations, and small IQN fits — all run with eval: true during the Quarto render. No separate scripts are needed.
Chapter 7: GBC surrogates. Train the IQN surrogate on benchmark functions (BGP, Friedman) and compare to GP baselines:
#| eval: false
python scripts/ch07_surrogates.py --dataset bgp --reps 50
python scripts/ch07_surrogates.py --dataset friedman --reps 50
Results are saved to cache/ch07_*.pt. Expected runtime: roughly 10 minutes on a GPU, 30 minutes on CPU.
Chapter 8: Jump discontinuities. The Aug-IQN pipeline for Phantom and Star:
#| eval: false
python scripts/ch08_jumps.py --dataset phantom --reps 10
python scripts/ch08_jumps.py --dataset star --reps 10
Expected results: Phantom RMSE \(\approx\) 0.044, CRPS \(\approx\) 0.009; Star RMSE \(\approx\) 0.059, CRPS \(\approx\) 0.013.
Chapter 9: Active learning. Run the randomized-prior acquisition loop:
#| eval: false
python scripts/ch09_active_learning.py --dataset rocket --n0 50 --budget 250 --reps 30
Expected: GBC RMSE \(\approx\) 0.007 vs. DGP baseline RMSE \(\approx\) 0.021 (roughly \(3\times\) improvement).
Chapter 14: Calibration (lake temperature). Train the het-MLP ensemble with temporal cross-validation conformal calibration:
#| eval: false
python scripts/ch14_lake.py --epochs 5000 --cv-folds 5
Expected: RMSE \(\approx\) 1.22, coverage \(\approx\) 90%, PI width \(\approx\) 3.8.
Once all cached results are in place, render the full book with:
quarto render
The rendered HTML appears in _book/. For PDF output:
quarto render --to pdf

B.5.1 Reproducing on a SLURM Cluster
The full experiment suite — especially the 30-replicate active learning runs and the 280k-row lake dataset — benefits from a SLURM-based HPC cluster with GPU nodes. We developed the book on the Hopper cluster at George Mason University, but any SLURM environment with NVIDIA GPUs will work.
Start by creating a Conda environment on the cluster’s shared filesystem so that all compute nodes see the same installation. Log into the head node and run:

Show code (6 lines)

module load anaconda3
conda create -n gbc python=3.12 -y
conda activate gbc
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121
cd /path/to/gbc-book
pip install -e ".[dev]"

We organize the training runs as a SLURM job array. Each array task trains one experimental configuration (dataset–replicate pair) on a single GPU. A template SLURM script looks like:

Show code (14 lines)

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gbc-train
#SBATCH --partition=gpuq
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --array=0-49
#SBATCH --output=logs/gbc_%A_%a.out

module load anaconda3
conda activate gbc

python scripts/ch07_surrogates.py --dataset bgp --rep $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

Save this as slurm/train_ch07.sh and submit with sbatch slurm/train_ch07.sh. The --array=0-49 flag launches 50 tasks, one per replicate. Each task writes its results to cache/ch07_bgp_rep{REP}.pt. Repeat for Chapters 8, 9, and 14 with analogous scripts.
After all jobs finish, collect the per-replicate files into a single summary. We provide a helper script that aggregates .pt files into the combined cache files that the chapter code expects:
python scripts/aggregate_cache.py --chapter 7
python scripts/aggregate_cache.py --chapter 8
python scripts/aggregate_cache.py --chapter 9
python scripts/aggregate_cache.py --chapter 14
Finally, render the book on the head node (or your local machine after copying the cache/ directory):
quarto render --to html
The Quarto render itself does not need a GPU. It only reads the cached .pt files and produces static HTML pages with embedded figures. A full render takes roughly five minutes on a modern laptop.

title: Appendix B — Computing Environment
text:
B.6 Troubleshooting
np.trapz not found. NumPy 2.0+ removed np.trapz. Use np.trapezoid instead. The gbc package handles this automatically, but if you encounter this error in your own code, update the function name.
PyTorch out of memory on GPU. Reduce batch size or use gradient accumulation. For the IQN, a batch size of 512 fits comfortably on a 4 GB GPU. If training the het-MLP ensemble on the lake dataset (280k rows), 8 GB of VRAM is recommended. On SLURM clusters, request a larger GPU partition (e.g., --gres=gpu:A100:1) if the default allocation is too small. You can also monitor memory usage in real time with nvidia-smi or torch.cuda.memory_summary() to identify which tensors consume the most VRAM.
CUDA version mismatch. If torch.cuda.is_available() returns False on a machine that has an NVIDIA GPU, the driver is likely too old for the CUDA runtime compiled into your PyTorch build. Run nvidia-smi to check the maximum supported CUDA version. Then reinstall PyTorch with a matching --index-url (e.g., cu118 instead of cu121). On shared clusters, the driver version is set by the sysadmin — contact them if it is out of date.
MPS backend errors on macOS. Some PyTorch operations are not yet implemented on MPS. If you encounter NotImplementedError, fall back to CPU by setting:
import os
os.environ["PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK"] = "1"
Quarto render hangs on a chapter. Chapters with eval: true code blocks execute during render. If a chapter appears to hang, it is likely training a model. Check execute: cache: true is set in _quarto.yml (it is by default) so that re-renders skip already-computed cells.
Results differ slightly from the book. Floating-point non-determinism across hardware is expected. Results should match to within reported standard errors. For exact reproduction, use the same GPU type (NVIDIA A100) and the PyTorch version pinned in pyproject.toml.
bibtex errors during PDF render. The bibliography file is references.bib. Quarto handles citation processing automatically. If you see undefined citation warnings, ensure you have run quarto render (not pdflatex directly).






Holthuijzen, Maike F., Robert B. Gramacy, Cayelan C. Carey, David M. Higdon, and R. Quinn Thomas. 2025. “Synthesizing Data Products, Mathematical Models, and Observations for Lake Temperature Forecasting.” Annals of Applied Statistics 19 (2). https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOAS1999.


Sauer, Annie, Robert B. Gramacy, and David Higdon. 2023. “Active Learning for Deep Gaussian Process Surrogates.” Technometrics 65 (1): 4–18. https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.2021.2008505.
